title: Emergent Specificity in Ubiquitin Chain Recognition: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode the Ubiquitin Code
title_norm: emergent specificity in ubiquitin chain recognition synthesizing structural and proteomic data to decode the ubiquitin code
abstract_text: Ubiquitin biology investigates how mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations produce distinct cellular signaling outcomes, which is important because specific linkages correspond to particular cellular functions despite low ubiquitin binding domain affinities. The mechanism by which multivalent cellular receptors selectively recognize specific polyubiquitin chain types remains an open question, particularly regarding how chain length and receptor mutations influence target specificity. The primary objective is to determine how mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations generate signaling specificity unachievable by monoubiquitin; this project will synthesize structural and proteomic datasets utilizing molecular dynamics simulations and graph neural networks. Resources including the Protein Data Bank, BioGRID, and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database will be integrated into a relational database utilizing ontology based annotation, UniProt mapping, and uniform conformational descriptor computations. The defined polyubiquitin chain recognition mechanisms will inform the design of targeted protein degradation therapeutics and identify the molecular basis of diseases linked to ubiquitin signaling dysregulation.
full_text: The proposed project within ubiquitin biology investigates how multivalent cellular receptors selectively recognize specific mesoscale polyubiquitin chain conformations. Current research connects distinct chain linkages to specific functions while structural data shows compact K48 and extended K63 architectures. The study determines how mesoscale conformations generate unique receptor specificity to advance therapeutic design for targeted protein degradation. The team integrates structural and proteomic datasets using molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning to predict cellular receptor selectivity. Key analytical methods include principal component analysis and graph neural networks alongside structural modeling through tools like HADDOCK. Results will undergo validation through five fold cross validation and testing against independent functional screens and nuclear magnetic resonance data. Data sources include the Protein Data Bank alongside functional interaction repositories like BioGRID and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The team will integrate these diverse sources into a relational database using ontology based annotation and standardized binding affinities. The absence of experimental structures for specific receptor complexes will be resolved using AlphaFold2 predictions and HADDOCK molecular docking. The three year timeline begins with data acquisition and progresses toward model development and final analysis of disease mutations. The extensive project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate necessary expertise in structural bioinformatics and computational chemistry methodologies. The researchers will publish open access papers and release all simulation code on GitHub alongside public data deposits in Zenodo. The collaborative team encompasses postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will gain extensive training in translational bioinformatics and synthesis methodologies.

The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and functional data exceeds single-lab capabilities. title_norm: emergent rna localization synthesizing spatial transcriptomics and rna structure data to model mrna targeting networks
abstract_text: Mesoscale cellular biology investigates the spatial localization of mRNA via RNA binding protein networks and RNA granules, a critical phenomenon currently mapped across large scale spatial, structural, and protein interaction datasets. This project will determine how RNA binding protein networks achieve precise mRNA targeting despite weak affinities by synthesizing diverse datasets using multi modal deep learning architectures, weighted correlation network analysis, community detection algorithms, and spatial statistics. The study will integrate databases including ENCODE, the Human Cell Atlas, and POSTAR3 by mapping transcript annotations to GENCODE v38, establishing unified coordinate systems, and applying platform specific normalization alongside batch correction. Uncovering these targeting mechanisms will elucidate membraneless organelle formation, outline the mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases linked to RNA binding protein mutations, and provide foundational parameters for mRNA therapeutics.
full_text: This project explores mesoscale cellular biology to understand how weak RNA binding networks and secondary structures direct mRNA localization. abstract_text: Structural and systems biology investigates bacterial microcompartments, wherein protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways to organize mesoscale metabolism, yielding extensive high resolution structural data on complete shells and building block proteins. This project will determine the physical principles governing microcompartment function through a computational synthesis utilizing finite element modeling in FEniCS, ordinary differential equation kinetic modeling via COPASI, and machine learning algorithms built with PyTorch Geometric. The research will integrate repositories including Protein Data Bank, BRENDA, and GenBank into a unified relational database by mapping structural data and kinetic parameters to specific proteins using UniProt accession numbers. Ultimately, this work will provide a mechanistic understanding of mesoscale cellular organization and yield the quantitative design rules required to engineer synthetic bacterial microcompartments for metabolic engineering applications.

The study will integrate datasets from the Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, and Human Cell Atlas by standardizing formats and aligning cross modality features through a hierarchical Bayesian framework. This research will provide a quantitative framework explaining how spatial organization dictates cellular decision making, which will advance immune response modeling and immunotherapy design for autoimmune diseases.

title: A Cross-Cell-Type Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Material States and Their Emergent Control of Gene Expression Noise
title_norm: a crosscelltype atlas of biomolecular condensate material states and their emergent control of gene expression noise
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through intrinsically disordered regions and multivalent interaction motifs, making their mesoscale material properties such as viscoelasticity and multiphase organization crucial for understanding cellular function. A critical scientific gap is the lack of quantitative predictive models explaining how specific sequence features dictate physical condensate states and systematically alter transcriptional bursting. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate material states control cell to cell gene expression noise by applying deep learning image segmentation, multimodal representation learning, and hierarchical Bayesian models to synthesize sequence, imaging, and single cell transcriptomic data. The approach will integrate databases including UniProt, the Human Protein Atlas, and the Human Cell Atlas, applying multiview representation learning to fuse sequence and imaging features into a unified latent space. This framework will connect physical condensate properties directly to emergent cellular phenotypes, providing a quantitative mechanism to explain context dependent gene regulation and disease related phase transitions.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Analytically, we will build a unified latent-variable model that maps composition/disorder/sequence grammars and imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, coarsening kinetics proxies, FRAP recovery parameters) onto a low-dimensional “material state manifold.” We will then connect that manifold to emergent transcriptional outcomes using hierarchical Bayesian models of bursting (inferring burst size/frequency from scRNA distributions), and causal discovery on perturbation datasets to identify regulators that shift condensates between states. Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Codes: Synthesizing Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics to Predict Organelle Contact Site Morphologies
title_norm: emergent membrane curvature codes synthesizing cryoet proteomics and lipidomics to predict organelle contact site morphologies
abstract_text: The research domain investigates membrane contact sites between organelles, focusing on how specific lipid compositions and diverse tethering proteins govern the mesoscale emergent properties of gap width, membrane curvature, and tether spacing. A unified geometric taxonomy of contact site morphotypes remains absent, and current biophysical models lack the parameterization necessary to predictively integrate molecular composition with structural geometry across different studies. This project will determine how combinations of lipids and tethering proteins generate mesoscale morphologies by applying discrete differential geometry, hierarchical Bayesian models, and multimodal graph neural networks to translate extracted imaging data into biophysical parameters. The analysis will integrate public databases including EMPIAR, EMDB, PRIDE, and AlphaFold using a metadata schema that standardizes condition variables and orthology mappings to produce derived physical feature tables and structural interaction graphs. Elucidating the precise relationship between molecular composition and morphology will explain how contact site geometry regulates lipid transfer, calcium microdomain formation, membrane remodeling, and organelle identity.

Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

abstract_original:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation

abstract_text: Mesoscale chromatin organization involves nanoscale domains and topological motifs that dictate essential gene regulatory behaviors like enhancer promoter communication and transcriptional bursting, representing a critical extension beyond traditional genome wide contact maps. To determine whether nanodomains organize into recurrent topological motifs driving cell type specific regulation, this project will synthesize multimodal datasets using multi resolution community detection, coarse grained polymer simulations, and unsupervised representation learning. Researchers will integrate ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, and 4D Nucleome Data Portal repositories by matching cell type ontologies, harmonizing genomic resolutions, and performing cross study calibration to construct joint multimodal feature vectors. This framework will produce a mesoscale model of chromatin regulation, converting descriptive structural catalogs into predictive knowledge by revealing the physical shapes underlying contact derived genomic patterns.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale chromatin organization lacks quantitative maps connecting physical nanodomains to shared topological motifs across diverse cell types. Existing contact maps provide geometric constraints but remain degenerate and fail to analyze combinations of structures for inferring regulatory behaviors. The study integrates imaging geometry with contact maps to determine if nanodomains form recurrent motifs driving regulatory behaviors of cells. This project for data synthesis builds pipelines to extract multimodal features and infer a dictionary of motifs predicting regulatory phenotypes. Methods include polymer simulations and community detection alongside representation learning and Bayesian regression to connect discovered motifs with regulatory phenotypes. The team validates results through replication across datasets and sensitivity analyses alongside benchmarking against known locus archetypes and published simulations. Data sources include the Human Cell Atlas and the BioImage Archive alongside public repositories like ENCODE and the GWAS Catalog. Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator: A Pan-Proteome Synthesis of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates
title_norm: protein crowding as an emergent mesoscale regulator a panproteome synthesis of cytoplasmic viscosity diffusion and reaction rates
abstract_text: Investigations into the physical properties of cellular interiors at the 10 to 1000 nanometer scale reveal that macromolecular density and viscosity drive complex diffusion behaviors critical across distinct cellular compartments and environmental states. To determine whether intracellular transport metrics can be mathematically derived from existing proteomic data, this project will synthesize multi omics and structural information into spatial crowding maps using obstruction scaling models, hierarchical Bayesian calibration, and gradient boosted trees. The study will integrate resources including ProteomeXchange, AlphaFold, and the Human Protein Atlas by linking UniProt identifiers and normalizing spatial compartments with Gene Ontology terms to calculate combined spatial probability arrays. This research will establish computational methods to infer spatial viscosity shifts directly from omics data, allowing intracellular transport speeds to be analyzed as physical outcomes of protein organization.
full_text: This project explores physical properties of cellular interiors at nanometer scales to determine if protein composition predicts transport metrics. Current evidence reveals that intracellular diffusion varies by compartment but mathematical links to molecular composition lack generalizable precision. The proposed study investigates if transport metrics derive mathematically from proteomic data to establish computational methods for inferring viscosity. The overall design aggregates existing data from multiple omics fields to construct spatial maps that link molecular composition to transport metrics. The team will apply fractional Brownian motion and hierarchical Bayesian calibration alongside gradient boosted trees and elastic net algorithms. The analytical approach validates these results through comparisons across datasets against published parameter estimates and posterior predictive checks. This project utilizes databases including the Human Protein Atlas and ProteomeXchange alongside structural archives like the Protein Data Bank. The synthesis plan integrates data by linking proteins via UniProt identifiers and normalizing compartments with Gene Ontology (GO) terms. The team mitigates inconsistent metadata formats by applying strict inclusion criteria and establishing rubrics for scoring quality of physical measurements. The timeline of thirty months progresses from initial data integration to physical modeling before concluding with software finalization and manuscripts. The broad scope requires collaboration across disciplines to combine domain knowledge spanning quantitative proteomics and soft matter theory. The team will distribute data archives and analysis pipelines with open source code via platforms including Zenodo and GitHub. The research group includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers alongside a software engineer and a graduate student receiving biophysics training.

abstract_original:
Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties—effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—arising from collective protein/RNA concentrations at 10–1000 nm scales. These properties shape signaling and metabolism but are not predictable from individual macromolecules. This project will test whether crowding-related emergent parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across organisms and conditions.

We will synthesize: (i) quantitative proteomics and absolute protein copy numbers (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB), (ii) subcellular localization and abundance maps (Human Protein Atlas; spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT in PRIDE), (iii) measurements of diffusion and viscosity from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, single-particle tracking, and FRAP compiled from public repositories and literature supplements (IDR/BioImage Archive; curated datasets), (iv) metabolomics that influences osmotic/crowding states (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) structural/biophysical properties of proteins (PDB, AlphaFold DB; predicted disorder from MobiDB; oligomerization from Complex Portal).

We will construct mesoscale “crowding fields” by combining spatial proteomics with protein size/shape estimates (from structures/predictions) to estimate excluded volume and soft interaction potentials in different compartments. We will fit these fields to observed diffusion/viscosity measurements using Bayesian calibration and coarse-grained physical models (e.g., obstruction scaling, fractional Brownian motion). Machine learning models will predict diffusion regimes for probe classes (enzymes, ribosomes, signaling proteins) given local proteome composition and interaction propensity.

Key questions: Do cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints in specific compartments (nucleoplasm vs cytosol) despite large proteome changes? Which protein classes (ribosomal proteins, chaperones, intrinsically disordered proteins) disproportionately control emergent viscosity? Can we predict condition-dependent shifts (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) in mesoscale diffusion landscapes from omics alone?

Expected insights include a quantitative, cross-species map linking proteome composition to emergent physical states, and identification of “crowding hubs” whose abundance changes re-tune global reaction kinetics. The project enables reinterpretation of many phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress) as consequences of mesoscale physical state changes.

This requires team science integrating quantitative proteomics, soft-matter physics, microscopy-based biophysics, and statistical learning, plus substantial data curation across heterogeneous measurement types. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate community standards for reporting diffusion/viscosity, build open databases of calibrated measurements, and deliver reproducible pipelines and training modules for a new generation of data-savvy biophysical cell biologists.

title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness
title_norm: emergent ribosome assembly landscapes integrating cryoem intermediates rrna processing maps and proteomics to explain assembly robustness
abstract_text: Ribosome biogenesis involves the assembly of mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates known as preribosomal particles, and studying this phenomenon explains how directional transitions, pathway robustness, and spatial organization emerge during assembly. A lack of integration across inconsistently annotated structural, sequencing, proteomic, and genetic datasets currently prevents linking structural snapshots to processing timelines, network redundancy, and specific assembly failure modes. This computational data synthesis project will construct a unified cross species assembly state graph mapping structural intermediates to processing events using probabilistic graphical models, consensus clustering algorithms, and Bayesian deconvolution methods. Data from repositories including the Protein Data Bank, UniProt, PRIDE, and ClinVar will be integrated by establishing a unified identifier mapping layer that links structural states to processing stages. The resulting assembly state graph will model ribosome biogenesis as a mesoscale network, providing a generalizable framework to explain tissue specific vulnerabilities in ribosomopathies and study other ribonucleoprotein complexes.
full_text: This study investigates the assembly of ribonucleoprotein intermediates to link isolated datasets with timelines of processing and system redundancy. Current data provide snapshots of assembly intermediates but lack synthesis to explain spatial organization and the robustness of pathways. The proposed study synthesizes public data to model ribosome assembly as a mesoscale network and explain vulnerabilities of tissues. This computational project probabilistically aligns structural consensus states with timelines of RNA processing and metrics of proteomic data. Key methods include algorithms for consensus clustering and probabilistic graphical models to analyze the controllability of the network. The team will validate results through checks of consistency across datasets and predictive evaluations on reserved structural datasets. The team will gather information from public databases including the Protein Data Bank and the Gene Expression Omnibus. The researchers will integrate distinct datasets by establishing a unified mapping layer to link structural states with stages of processing. The project will mitigate inconsistent annotations across studies by calculating standardized descriptors of conformation from raw structural data. The proposed timeline spans thirty months to complete initial ingestion of data and conclude with finalization of public resources. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide simultaneous expertise in structural biology and the modeling of networks. The team will ensure public availability by sharing open source code and deploying a web portal with open tutorials. The team features principal investigators and graduate research assistants who will receive instruction across multiple distinct scientific disciplines.

abstract_original:
Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

We will build a unified “assembly state graph” where nodes are structural intermediates (from cryo-EM) and edges represent transitions constrained by rRNA processing events and factor binding/unbinding. Using probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts, we will infer transition probabilities and identify bottlenecks. Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.

Hypotheses: (1) assembly robustness emerges from redundant, partially ordered modules that buffer factor loss; (2) specific mesoscale nucleolar subcompartments correspond to distinct regions of the assembly state graph; and (3) disease mutations in ribosomopathies disproportionately affect transitions with low redundancy, explaining tissue-specific vulnerability.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

title: Mesoscale Signaling Microclusters as Emergent Computation: A Synthesis of Immune Receptor Imaging, Phosphoproteomics, and Single-Cell Responses
title_norm: mesoscale signaling microclusters as emergent computation a synthesis of immune receptor imaging phosphoproteomics and singlecell responses
abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular immunology, mesoscale immune receptor microclusters at the plasma membrane enrich kinases and couple to the cytoskeleton to crucially regulate downstream signaling dynamics and single cell outcomes. Because existing multimodal data remain fragmented across isolated modalities, the field lacks generalizable mechanistic models that map spatial architecture to emergent response modes. The primary objective is to determine how mesoscale organization controls immune activation; this project will utilize computer vision, point process statistics, and dynamical systems modeling to mathematically link standardized image features to phosphorylation trajectories. The study will synthesize datasets from repositories including the Image Data Resource, PRIDE, and Gene Expression Omnibus via a mediation framework where image derived features act as covariates predicting phosphoproteomic dynamical coefficients. This research will identify universal structural motifs that provide mechanistic explanations for heterogeneous single cell responses, thereby establishing spatial organization as the primary driver of signaling outcomes.
full_text: The domain of molecular immunology lacks models to link mesoscale microclusters of immune receptors to emergent response modes. Receptors regulate signaling by organizing kinases but the downstream effects of spatial arrangements on single cells remain incomplete. The primary objective explores how spatial organization controls immune activation to explain the heterogeneous responses of single cells. The computational synthesis of data harmonizes public datasets to link spatial features with trajectories of phosphorylation and activation. The analytical approach applies computer vision and statistics of point processes alongside hierarchical models of Bayesian latent variables. The project validates results through evaluation of cross study performance and analysis of sensitivity using computationally degraded images. The study incorporates information from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) alongside datasets of microscopy. A unified schema of metadata integrates diverse resources by using spatial features to predict coefficients of dynamic signaling. The team mitigates variations of experimental resolution and sampling through rule based harmonization and regression of Gaussian processes. The timeline of thirty months includes early release of pipelines before completing models of multiscale dynamics and benchmarks. This ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide concurrent expertise in quantitative immunology and engineering of software. The team will release open access papers and deposit open source code in repositories like GitHub and Zenodo. The research group includes primary investigators and postdoctoral scholars who provide trainees with cross disciplinary mentorship and support.

abstract_original:
Immune receptors form mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) at the plasma membrane that act as emergent computational units, integrating ligand binding, mechanical forces, and feedback to produce switch-like or graded activation. The emergent phenomenon is that collective receptor organization and kinase/phosphatase partitioning yields signaling behaviors not predictable from receptor–ligand affinity alone.

We will synthesize: (i) TCR/BCR and Fc receptor super-resolution and TIRF imaging datasets with cluster statistics (IDR, BioImage Archive; published single-molecule localization microscopy datasets), (ii) phosphoproteomics time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) single-cell functional readouts (CyTOF and flow cytometry in ImmPort; scRNA-seq activation time courses in GEO), (iv) ligand affinity/kinetics and epitope data (IEDB; structural complexes in PDB), and (v) perturbation datasets for kinases, phosphatases, and cytoskeletal regulators (DepMap; LINCS small-molecule perturbations).

Analytically, we will develop a multiscale model linking microcluster architecture to downstream phosphorylation and transcription. Computer vision and point-process statistics will quantify cluster size distributions, lifetimes, and nanoscale colocalization of signaling proteins. We will integrate these features with phosphoproteomic trajectories via dynamical systems identification (sparse regression / SINDy) and with single-cell outcomes using mixture models to capture heterogeneous activation states. A key goal is to infer whether there exist universal “microcluster motifs” (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells) that correspond to distinct emergent response modes.

Hypotheses: (1) microcluster morphology encodes a mesoscale “gain control” that determines sensitivity vs specificity; (2) cytoskeletal coupling shifts microcluster systems between excitable and bistable regimes; and (3) disease-associated variants in signaling proteins act by altering partitioning into clusters rather than changing catalytic rates.

Expected insights include predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and functional immune outcomes, a cross-study standardized microcluster feature set, and mechanistic explanations for disparate experimental results in the literature. This requires team science spanning immunology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, plus significant synthesis to harmonize stimulation protocols and imaging modalities.

NCEMS support is essential to convene communities, build open pipelines for microcluster quantification, and create an openly accessible benchmark dataset and modeling toolkit. Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary training in image analysis, omics integration, and reproducible computational immunology.

title: Emergent Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics: Integrating Cryo-ET, Live Imaging, and Proteogenomics to Explain Bioenergetic Plasticity
title_norm: emergent mitochondrial cristae morphodynamics integrating cryoet live imaging and proteogenomics to explain bioenergetic plasticity
abstract_text: The mesoscale geometry and topology of mitochondrial cristae govern cellular energy production, shaped by key proteins that restrict diffusion, generate membrane curvature, and regulate membrane fusion. This project will determine conserved cristae states and their molecular drivers by computationally analyzing public data using convolutional neural networks, persistent homology, causal inference modeling, and physics based generative algorithms to explain respiratory differences. Extracted physical features from databases including EMPIAR, EMDB, and single cell atlases will be merged with molecular and functional datasets like ENCODE using unified metadata schemas, causal graphs, and multi task learning. The resulting mathematical framework will shift cristae analysis from qualitative observation to quantitative measurement, formally linking molecular composition and physical structure to cellular respiratory output.
full_text: The research domain covers the mesoscale geometry of mitochondrial cristae and the absence of models linking structure and respiration. The primary objective identifies conserved structural states and molecular drivers to provide a mathematical framework linking composition and respiratory output. The study design relies on the computational synthesis of existing public data to build predictive and physical models. The analytical approach applies convolutional neural networks for image segmentation and generative models utilizing equations of membrane bending energy. The team will validate the generated models through replication across datasets and the verification against established biological controls. The project will utilize diverse public databases including EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library alongside single cell atlases. The team will integrate these databases by extracting physical features from images and merging them using causal graphs. The researchers will address the common limitations of missing image segmentations by generating them utilizing open source algorithms. The proposed study spans thirty months to complete the initial data processing and the final synthesis for publication. The integration of imaging and membrane physics requires cross disciplinary collaboration to exceed the limits of single laboratories. The project will release open access datasets and open source software libraries to ensure the availability of findings. The team includes specialists of imaging and graduate students receiving cross disciplinary training across multiple distinct scientific domains.

abstract_original:
Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds (20–100 nm curvature radii; 10–30 nm junctions) whose collective organization determines respiratory efficiency and signaling. The emergent phenomenon is that cristae architecture—junction density, lamellar vs tubular balance, and local protein crowding—produces nonlinear changes in bioenergetic output not predictable from individual OXPHOS complexes.

We will synthesize public datasets: (i) cryo-ET reconstructions and segmentations of cristae across conditions and organisms (EMPIAR, EMDB), (ii) live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics and cristae reporters where available (IDR/BioImage Archive; Mitochondria Dynamics datasets), (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics of mitochondrial fractions and MICOS/OPA1/ATP synthase oligomers (PRIDE), (iv) genomics and transcriptomics for mitochondrial-shaping genes (GTEx, ENCODE; scRNA-seq atlases), and (v) functional readouts of respiration (public Seahorse datasets and compiled literature values; gene perturbation phenotypes in DepMap).

We will quantify mesoscale cristae geometry from cryo-ET via curvature analysis, junction graph extraction, and topology measures (surface genus, connectivity). We will integrate these with proteomic abundance of shaping complexes and with genetic perturbation effects using causal inference and multi-task learning. Physics-informed models of membrane elasticity and protein-induced curvature will be calibrated to explain observed morphotypes and predict transitions.

Central questions: Are there conserved cristae “architectural states” across cell types that correspond to distinct metabolic regimes? Which combinations of MICOS components, ATP synthase dimerization, and OPA1 processing drive state transitions? Can we explain why similar proteomic changes yield different functional outcomes in different tissues as a consequence of mesoscale geometry constraints?

Expected insights include an atlas of cristae architectural states, quantitative links between shaping complex stoichiometry and emergent cristae topology, and mechanistic hypotheses for mitochondrial diseases where morphology and function decouple. Methodological advances will include open-source tools for extracting standardized geometric descriptors from tomograms.

The project demands collaboration between cryo-ET experts, mitochondrial biologists, membrane physicists, and machine learning scientists, and requires extensive synthesis of heterogeneous structural and omics data beyond a single lab’s capability. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, open workflows, and trainee training in quantitative 3D ultrastructure analysis and integrative modeling.

title: Mesoscale Assembly of Viral Replication Compartments: A Cross-Virus Synthesis of Host Factor Recruitment and Emergent Replication Efficiency
title_norm: mesoscale assembly of viral replication compartments a crossvirus synthesis of host factor recruitment and emergent replication efficiency
abstract_text: Virology and cellular mesoscale organization investigate viral replication compartments, which comprise membrane bound organelles or membraneless inclusions whose formation mechanisms hold crucial importance for understanding diverse RNA and DNA viruses. Currently, knowledge remains fragmented across subfields, and researchers do not understand whether compartment architecture and recruited host protein modules share universal design principles that determine viral replication efficiency. This project will establish predictive relationships between compartment features and host modules by applying deep learning image processing, network analysis algorithms, and causal modeling to synthesize public data and determine universal design principles. The study will integrate diverse repositories including BioImage Archive, BioGRID, and AlphaFold DB by utilizing controlled vocabularies, unified metadata schemas, and joint feature embeddings to align imaging datasets and transcriptomic profiles. This framework will elucidate generalizable principles of cellular organization across viral species and identify conserved host organizer modules that function as broad spectrum antiviral targets.
full_text: This project in virology and cellular mesoscale organization questions whether diverse compartments of viral replication share universal design principles. Researchers understand the structural variation of compartments across viruses but lack standardized metrics and integrated analyses of host networks. The proposed study links features of compartments with host modules to uncover targets for broad spectrum antiviral therapies. This computational study synthesizes existing data to link features of images and networks with phenotypes of viral replication. The team will apply tools like U-Net for images and node2vec for networks alongside models of hierarchical regression. Researchers will validate results using independent datasets and cross validation while benchmarking against external references and randomized negative controls. The project leverages public databases including BioImage Archive and BioGRID alongside references like Reactome and the Protein Data Bank. The team will integrate these diverse datasets through a unified metadata schema and temporal alignment of images and transcripts. The researchers will mitigate differences across laboratories and modalities through models for batch effects and calculations of effect sizes. This thirty month project includes sequential milestones to harmonize metadata and develop predictive models before releasing code and data. The ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to harmonize and analyze distinct modalities of data across numerous viral species. The researchers will deposit data and pipelines in repositories like Zenodo and publish findings in open access scientific journals. This team includes scientists and trainees from diverse disciplines to foster cross disciplinary training in reproducible computational workflows.

Many viruses create mesoscale replication compartments (100–1000 nm membraneless inclusions or membrane-bound organelles) that concentrate viral and host factors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective compartment organization yields replication efficiencies and immune evasion strategies not predictable from individual viral proteins. This project will ask whether replication compartments share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses.

We will synthesize: (i) viral replication compartment imaging datasets (electron microscopy and fluorescence) from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, spanning RNA viruses (coronaviruses, flaviviruses) and DNA viruses (herpesviruses), (ii) host–virus protein interaction networks (IntAct, BioGRID, VirHostNet), (iii) CRISPR and RNAi screens for host dependency factors (DepMap viral screens; published screens in GEO/SRA), (iv) viral and host transcriptomic responses (GEO; single-cell infection atlases where available), and (v) structural data for viral scaffold proteins and host recruited complexes (PDB, AlphaFold DB).

We will develop a comparative mesoscale compartment feature framework: size distributions, internal subcompartmentalization, proximity to organelles, and dynamics proxies. Using network embedding and community detection on host–virus interactomes, we will identify recurrent host modules (e.g., RNA metabolism, membrane trafficking, stress granule components) recruited into compartments. We will then relate these modules to compartment morphotypes and to replication phenotypes (viral titers/replication markers from public datasets) using multi-level regression and causal graph methods.

Hypotheses: (1) replication compartments implement convergent mesoscale strategies—phase separation, membrane curvature scaffolding, or hybrid forms—to optimize reaction kinetics and shield nucleic acids; (2) the emergent efficiency depends on a small number of host module recruitments that act as “mesoscale organizers”; and (3) antiviral perturbations that disrupt mesoscale organization (rather than single enzymes) provide broad-spectrum leverage.

Expected insights include a cross-virus taxonomy of replication compartment architectures, identification of conserved host mesoscale organizers, and predictive models linking host factor modules to compartment type and replication success. Deliverables will include open compartment feature datasets and interoperable pipelines for image and network integration.

This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.

title: Emergent Cell Wall Nanomechanics: Synthesizing Fungal and Plant Cell Wall Composition, Ultrastructure, and Growth Patterns
title_norm: emergent cell wall nanomechanics synthesizing fungal and plant cell wall composition ultrastructure and growth patterns
abstract_text: The mesoscale organization of plant and fungal cell walls dictates emergent mechanical properties such as stiffness and fracture behavior, but isolated data and protocol heterogeneity prevent unified synthesis across these biological domains. A significant gap remains in developing cross kingdom predictive models and generalizable principles that connect biochemical composition and enzyme activity to ultrastructural organization and mechanical responses. This project will synthesize multi omics and imaging data using Bayesian meta analysis, Fourier domain methods, and gradient boosted trees to determine universal mesoscale design principles and build integrative models linking molecular inputs to mechanical outputs. Information from databases including CAZy, FungiDB, EMPIAR, and the BioImage Archive will be integrated into a unified semantic knowledge graph using standard cross reference identifier mapping and explicit versioning. This research will establish quantitative relationships linking molecular changes to cellular outcomes, providing mechanistic explanations for crop resilience, pathogen infection, and biological nanocomposite behavior independent of simple gene lists.
full_text: This project investigates mesoscale architecture in plant and fungal cell walls to build missing cross kingdom predictive models. Extensive catalogs of biosynthetic enzymes exist but heterogeneous experimental protocols keep structural data isolated and prevent direct comparisons. The study asks if these walls share universal design principles to mechanistically explain crop resilience and pathogen infection. This secondary data synthesis extracts architectural descriptors from public datasets to build models of molecular inputs and outputs. Methods include structure tensor analysis and gradient boosted trees alongside multilevel Bayesian models to evaluate the curated data. The team validates results through nested cross validation and posterior predictive checks alongside positive controls using known mutants. Data sources include genetic databases (UniProtKB) and structural repositories (BioImage Archive) alongside public files from Zenodo and Figshare. The project integrates these datasets into a knowledge graph by using explicit versioning and schemas for identifier mapping. The team will address missing imaging data and protocol heterogeneity by deploying hierarchical Bayesian harmonization and latent variable models. The thirty month timeline progresses from initial data curation and pipeline development to final predictive modeling and atlas releases. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating biology with machine learning exceeds the capacity of one laboratory. The team will release an open source public atlas alongside containerized analytical workflows and complete data depositions on Zenodo. The diverse team includes physicists and early career biologists who will receive collaborative training through virtual tutorial series.

abstract_original:
Cell walls are mesoscale composite materials (10–500 nm fibril bundles, crosslinks, and pores) whose emergent mechanical properties enable growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polysaccharide architecture produces nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior not predictable from monomer composition. This project will synthesize multi-omics and imaging data to uncover universal principles of cell wall nanocomposite design in plants and fungi.

We will integrate: (i) cell wall compositional datasets (glycomics and carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations from CAZy; polysaccharide composition in Metabolomics Workbench and literature-derived datasets), (ii) solid-state NMR and scattering data where publicly available (BMRB; published SAXS/WAXS datasets), (iii) AFM nanomechanics maps and electron microscopy of wall ultrastructure (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (iv) transcriptomics of wall biosynthesis during growth and stress (GEO; Arabidopsis eFP, fungal expression atlases), and (v) mutant/perturbation phenotypes affecting morphology (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content imaging screens).

Analytically, we will build a mesoscale structure–property model linking polymer composition and enzyme expression to ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation, bundling, pore size distributions) and to mechanical outputs (Young’s modulus maps, viscoelastic parameters). We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Which crosslink motifs (e.g., lignin–cellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) create emergent anisotropic growth? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

title: Mesoscale Proteasome and Autophagy Hub Organization: Integrating Spatial Proteomics, Imaging, and Ubiquitinome Data to Explain Proteostasis Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale proteasome and autophagy hub organization integrating spatial proteomics imaging and ubiquitinome data to explain proteostasis emergence
abstract_text: The proteostasis research domain focuses on the mesoscale organization of degradation hubs, including proteasome rich microdomains and autophagy initiation sites, which operate as crucial structures for maintaining cellular protein balance. However, spatial imaging phenotypes remain isolated from ubiquitin linkage data and spatial proteomics, leaving the connection between molecular components and system level aggregation behaviors unclear. This project will determine how mesoscale hub architectures generate system level proteostasis behaviors by synthesizing multi omics datasets utilizing image segmentation, spatial statistics, hierarchical Bayesian meta analysis, and dynamical modeling. The research will integrate diverse datasets from repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, PRIDE Archive, and Image Data Resource by building a standardized metadata schema and applying Similarity Network Fusion. This framework will yield candidate mesoscale biomarkers for proteostasis failure, establishing spatial organization as an intermediate layer connecting molecular functions to cell level robustness.
full_text: The scientific domain of proteostasis investigates the mesoscale organization of degradation hubs and its connection to ubiquitin linkage chemistry. Research establishes that proteostasis operates via mesoscale hubs but the integration of spatial imaging with ubiquitin data remains incomplete. The proposed study asks how mesoscale hub organization generates system level behaviors to reveal novel biomarkers for neurodegenerative disease. The core analytical strategy employs a non experimental synthesis to integrate public datasets using a standardized metadata schema. Methods include algorithms for image segmentation and spatial statistics alongside models of dynamical systems and Similarity Network Fusion. Researchers will validate results through cross dataset replication and predictive modeling applied to held out datasets and independent databases. The project will utilize datasets from the Human Protein Atlas and the Image Data Resource alongside the PRIDE Archive. Distinct databases will be integrated by building a standardized metadata schema to map shared cell lines and perturbations. The research team will mitigate inconsistent metadata and incomplete dataset overlap by standardizing schemas and applying rigorous sensitivity checks. The thirty month project timeline progresses from finalizing metadata schemas to scaling feature extraction and integrating phenotypic databases. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in quantitative bioimage analysis and statistical multi omics integration. The researchers will distribute findings by depositing datasets in Zenodo and releasing open source code through public web portals. The team comprises principal investigators and trainees across multiple disciplines who will receive cross disciplinary training via code sprints.

abstract_original:
Proteostasis emerges from mesoscale organization of degradation hubs—proteasome-rich microdomains, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation sites (50–1000 nm)—that coordinate substrate selection, sequestration, and clearance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial organization and phase-like sequestration yields system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, not predictable from individual E3 ligases or proteases.

We will synthesize: (i) spatial proteomics identifying proteasome/autophagy component localization (Human Protein Atlas; hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets in PRIDE), (ii) ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover datasets (PRIDE; ubiquitin linkage-specific studies), (iii) bioimaging of aggresomes, p62 bodies, autophagosome markers, and proteasome foci (IDR/BioImage Archive), (iv) genetic perturbation screens for proteostasis regulators (DepMap; CRISPR screens for aggregation/toxicity), and (v) disease datasets with proteostasis failure signatures (AMP-AD proteomics; ALS/FTD proteomics and transcriptomics in GEO).

We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

title: Emergent Bacterial Microcompartment Design Rules: Synthesizing Genomes, Structures, and Metabolic Flux to Predict Organelle-Like Function
title_norm: emergent bacterial microcompartment design rules synthesizing genomes structures and metabolic flux to predict organellelike function
abstract_text: Bacterial microcompartments are polyhedral protein based organelles that encapsulate enzymes to alter metabolic flux, highlighting the importance of understanding how mesoscale organization and pore properties create selective microenvironments. This project will build a comparative computational framework linking genetic composition to metabolic function by applying machine learning, assembly modeling, and reaction diffusion simulations to predict pore properties, infer shell architecture, and determine permeability motifs. The study will integrate diverse structural and metabolic datasets from Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, and KEGG by building a standardized identifier mapping layer stored across relational and graph database architectures. This research will deliver a predictive framework establishing general principles of chemical microenvironment construction, generating structural and functional insights broadly applicable to other mesoscale biological assemblies like viral capsids.
full_text: This project explores the mesoscale organization of bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to resolve missing maps for properties of pores and shells. These polyhedral organelles encapsulate enzymes to alter metabolic flux but mechanisms connecting clusters of genes to structural geometry remain unclear. The primary question asks how genetic composition determines the architecture of shells to provide predictive models for other biological structures. The study design features a computational synthesis of public datasets to predict properties of pores and simulate gradients of metabolites. The analytical approach applies hidden Markov models for the detection of loci and gradient boosted trees to evaluate genomic features. Results will be validated by comparing predictions of motifs against established structures and benchmarking models against published data from metabolomics. The project will utilize databases of sequences including UniProt and repositories of structures such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Distinct datasets will be integrated through a mapping layer of identifiers stored within a relational database and graph database. Known uncertainties of predictions for structures will be mitigated by filtering data with confidence scores and utilizing Bayesian inference. The project spans thirty months and includes milestones for releasing an atlas of loci and developing computational pipelines. This extensive scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to successfully integrate specialized expertise in microbial genomics and machine learning. The researchers will share findings through open access manuscripts and release open source code and data on public repositories. The team incorporates principal investigators and graduate students to offer computational training opportunities across multiple distinct career stages.

abstract_original:
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles (50–300 nm) whose emergent permeability and enzyme colocalization enable metabolic pathways that would be inefficient or toxic in the cytosol. The emergent phenomenon is that shell protein assembly and pore organization generate selective transport and reaction microenvironments not predictable from individual enzymes.

We will synthesize: (i) BMC gene clusters across bacterial genomes (NCBI RefSeq, IMG; curated BMC databases), (ii) shell protein and encapsulated enzyme structures (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) metabolomics and flux measurements for BMC-associated pathways (Metabolomics Workbench; published 13C flux studies), (iv) cryo-EM structures of intact BMCs and shells (EMDB/EMPIAR), and (v) environmental metadata and phenotypes for host organisms (GOLD database; literature-derived growth phenotypes).

We will build a comparative framework linking genetic composition to mesoscale shell architecture and emergent function. First, we will annotate shell protein families and predict pore properties (charge, diameter, gating motifs) from structures. Second, we will infer likely shell stoichiometries and tessellation patterns using assembly modeling and constraints from cryo-EM. Third, we will integrate pathway enzyme kinetics (from BRENDA) with predicted permeability to simulate emergent metabolite gradients and flux enhancement using reaction–diffusion models. Machine learning will map gene cluster features to predicted organelle performance metrics (toxicity mitigation, flux gain).

Key questions: Are there universal shell “permeability motifs” that recur across unrelated BMC types? How do small changes in pore composition produce emergent switches between retention vs throughput regimes? Can we predict ecological niches where particular BMC designs confer advantage?

Expected insights include design rules for emergent mesoscale selectivity, a taxonomy of BMC architectures linked to metabolic outcomes, and open tools for predicting BMC function from genomes. While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

title: Mesoscale Vesicle Coat Self-Organization: Integrating Structural Proteomics and Imaging to Explain Cargo Selectivity Emergence
title_norm: mesoscale vesicle coat selforganization integrating structural proteomics and imaging to explain cargo selectivity emergence
abstract_text: Vesicular trafficking relies on the mesoscale self organization of vesicle coats into lattices, a fundamental biological phenomenon that dictates cargo selectivity and vesicle size via established individual molecular interactions. This project will determine how mesoscale self organization generates emergent cargo selectivity by constructing an integrative atlas, applying graph based community detection, coarse grained physics informed simulations, and Bayesian networks to harmonize existing public datasets. The study will integrate databases including PDB, EMDB, PRIDE, and BioGRID into a multi modal knowledge graph by mapping proteins to UniProt accessions and standardizing metadata to link structural and genetic interactions. This output will provide predictive principles of mesoscale self organization, replacing descriptive cargo selection models with quantitative thresholds to inform downstream cellular function and disease research.

The primary question explores how coat organization drives selectivity to establish predictive principles across systems that replace purely descriptive models. abstract_original:
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize disparate datasets, build open analysis pipelines, and train trainees to integrate structure, networks, and bioimage-derived mesoscale phenotypes under reproducible open science.

title: Emergent Nuclear Pore Selectivity at the Mesoscale: A Synthesis of FG-Nup Disorder, Transport Kinetics, and NPC Ultrastructure
title_norm: emergent nuclear pore selectivity at the mesoscale a synthesis of fgnup disorder transport kinetics and npc ultrastructure
abstract_text: The selective nucleocytoplasmic transport domain focuses on the nuclear pore complex and its FG nucleoporin permeability barrier, which is important for explaining the mesoscale emergence of selectivity from extensive public data. This project will build a multiscale model to infer mesoscale parameters governing nuclear pore complex selectivity by linking sequence and structural data to coarse grained polymer simulations using hierarchical Bayesian inference and neural posterior estimation. Diverse public databases including Protein Data Bank, UniProt, ClinVar, and published transport kinetics will be integrated into a versioned knowledge graph that normalizes biological conditions and maps structural components to functional data. This framework will yield a novel multiscale model that reframes disease mutations as shifts in collective material properties, establishing fundamental principles applicable to other intrinsically disordered protein systems.
full_text: This project investigates the nuclear pore complex to determine whether divergent sequences of FG nucleoporins implement conserved designs of the barrier. Abundant public data regarding structures and kinetics exist but remain unintegrated to explain the emergence of selectivity at the mesoscale. Key methods include simulations of coarse grained polymers and neural posterior estimation alongside techniques for hierarchical Bayesian inference. The team validates results using hold out validation on matched datasets and comparisons of inferred dimensions against independent structural measurements. The project utilizes databases including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and UniProt alongside published sets of kinetics for transport. The team shares curated data through public repositories and releases an open source toolkit alongside a versioned knowledge graph. Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.
