title: Nuclear Speckles as Splicing Hubs: Emergent Amplification of Gene Expression
title_norm: nuclear speckles as splicing hubs emergent amplification of gene expression
abstract_text: Within the domain of nuclear biology, nuclear speckles are phase separated condensates containing splicing factors that play a crucial role in altering RNA splicing efficiency through spatial organization. The open scientific gap is the quantitative relationship between physical distance to nuclear speckles and RNA splicing rates, because existing data remain unsynthesized regarding how proximity impacts processing kinetics. The primary objective will determine if spatial distance dictates splicing efficiency for multi intron genes across cell types by integrating secondary data utilizing generalized additive models, graph neural networks, and biophysical two phase kinetic modeling. Genomic, transcriptomic, and super resolution microscopy datasets from ENCODE and 4D Nucleome Data Portal will merge into a unified vector structure associating speckle distance scores with splicing and transcription rates. This research will output a novel framework demonstrating whether three dimensional spatial positioning relative to nuclear bodies serves as an independent variable predicting RNA processing beyond linear DNA sequences.

title: Synthetic Cell Assembly: Predicting Emergent Life-like Behaviors from Component Integration
title_norm: synthetic cell assembly predicting emergent lifelike behaviors from component integration
abstract_text: The bottom up synthetic biology domain investigates the minimal requirements for emergent behaviors such as motility and division in synthetic cells, requiring an integrated mesoscale understanding of kinetic, structural, and omics data. Currently, the field lacks the ability to predict emergent system failures, such as membrane lysis and transcription stalling, that occur when integrating isolated genetic and membrane components. This project will synthesize existing data to train machine learning models predicting system stability through a computational meta synthesis that will integrate metabolic flux and biophysical membrane models utilizing graph neural networks, physics informed neural networks, and Bayesian inference. Datasets from the BioModels Database, BRENDA, LipidMaps, and SynBioHub will be integrated by standardizing metadata to construct a knowledge graph mapping molecular components and interactions weighted by kinetic parameters derived from literature. The resulting predictive framework will transition synthetic cell construction from trial and error processes to rational design and identify fundamental biophysical constraints relevant to self replication and life origins.

The overall design is a computational synthesis of public data integrating models of metabolic flux and biophysical membranes. Key methods include Bayesian inference and neural networks alongside the standardization of metadata using the Synthetic Biology Open Language. The team validates results computationally through cross validation by evaluating predictions against unpublished negative data from failed experimental constructs. This project uses multiple public datasets from the BioModels Database and SynBioHub alongside community repositories like the PRIDE archives. This project spans two years and six months to complete data harvesting before finalizing model training and computational validation. title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Mesoscale Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Phase Behavior, Interactome Architecture, and Cellular Function

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation depend on specific protein sequence features to establish mesoscale material properties, making the unification of fragmented biophysical data essential for predictive modeling. Currently, no proteome scale framework links protein sequence features to emergent material states and multiphase architectures, leaving the mechanisms driving functional and disease related outcomes fundamentally uncharacterized. This project will develop the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas through a computational synthesis utilizing gradient boosted trees, graph neural networks, and network based algorithms to identify sequence and interaction rules predicting material states and disease disruptions. Data from resources including PhaSepDB, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas will be programmatically extracted, standardized using UniProt identifiers, and assembled into a relational database linking structural metadata directly to protein sequences. abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to organelle-scale structures with distinct material properties (liquid, gel, solid) that dictate cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects sequence-encoded molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material states and their functional/pathological consequences across the proteome. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize eight distinct public data ecosystems—(1) condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), (2) IDR and phase-separation propensity predictors (PScore, catGRANULE, FuzDrop), (3) genome-scale interactome and co-complex data (BioGRID, STRING, hu.MAP), (4) subcellular localization atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell live-imaging library), (5) structural data from cryo-EM/ET of cellular condensates (EMDB), (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived material-property measurements curated from literature, (7) disease mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-forming proteins, and (8) evolutionary conservation data (UniProt, Pfam) across species. By integrating these previously siloed resources, we will build a computational framework—the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas (CoMA)—that links sequence features to predicted material properties, interactome connectivity, and functional/disease outcomes at proteome scale. Specific aims include: (1) constructing a harmonized, machine-readable dataset unifying sequence, structural, biophysical, and phenotypic condensate data for >2,000 human proteins; (2) applying interpretable machine learning and network-based approaches to identify sequence and interaction motifs (the 'molecular grammar') that predict emergent material states and multiphase organization (e.g., core-shell condensates); (3) testing whether disease-associated mutations preferentially disrupt predicted grammar features linked to material-state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer; and (4) validating framework predictions against independent public datasets not used in model training. This task exceeds single-lab capacity: it requires biophysicists who understand phase-separation thermodynamics, structural biologists interpreting cryo-EM data, computational biologists building predictive models, cell biologists validating localization/functional data, and clinicians/geneticists linking findings to disease—expertise no single laboratory possesses. NCEMS support is essential to provide computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, differently formatted datasets, to convene the necessary interdisciplinary expertise, and to establish shared open-science standards for reproducible mesoscale data synthesis. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis pipelines will be released as FAIR, versioned resources via GitHub and Zenodo, accompanied by interactive visualization tools for the broader community. The Working Group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computational biology, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning interpretability, and collaborative open-science workflows—directly cultivating the data-savvy, cross-disciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis effort promises to resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how simple sequence-encoded interactions give rise to complex, function-defining mesoscale organization, with direct implications for understanding proteinopathies and designing synthetic condensates.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

This Working Group will synthesize five major public resources: (1) sequence-based condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS) and IDR predictors (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct); (3) high-resolution subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting); (4) structural and AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles for disordered/multivalent proteins; and (5) disease-mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-associated proteins. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.

Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. All curated datasets, ontologies, trained models, and analysis code will be released as open-access community resources via Zenodo/GitHub, with a living database designed for continuous community contribution. By synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—how simple molecular rules generate complex emergent condensate behavior—while generating a foundational, reusable resource for the mesoscale biology community.

abstract_text: The research domain centers on biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA, and post translational modifications drive material properties dictating cellular functions. The primary objective is to identify combinatorial molecular rules dictating material properties and cellular outcomes; achieving this will involve training graph neural networks and gradient boosted trees utilizing structural embeddings and SHAP based feature attribution. This project will integrate diverse datasets including PhaSepDB, AlphaFold DB, UniProt, and BioGRID into a relational database utilizing a controlled vocabulary ontology to standardize protein identifiers, condensate labels, and metadata with continuous provenance tracking. Identifying these molecular rules will yield a generalizable framework for predicting condensate behavior, providing quantitative parameters to direct future condensate engineering and targeted therapeutics across the biomedical field.
full_text: This research investigates biomolecular condensates to provide missing frameworks connecting molecular features with material properties across disconnected repositories of data. The combinatorial determination of material properties remains poorly understood despite abundant data regarding individual components of biomolecular condensates. The primary question explores how molecular rules dictate material properties to yield generalizable frameworks for targeted therapeutics and engineering. The core strategy builds a unified meta database of proteins and trains computational models to predict specific material properties. Key models include graph neural networks and gradient boosted trees alongside standardized pipelines for segmentation and tracking of droplets. The researchers will validate findings through nested cross validation and correlation with published measurements of parameters like kinetics of fusion. This project extracts datasets from repositories including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside the Human Protein Atlas and COSMIC. The team will merge distinct datasets into a relational meta database utilizing a controlled vocabulary ontology for standardization. The researchers will algorithmically extract morphological features to mitigate the lack of biophysical parameters within existing databases of images. The timeline features quarterly workshops for harmonization organized around modular sprints for database construction and subsequent development of predictive models. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine concurrent expertise in polymer physics and machine learning for massive datasets. The researchers will publish open access preprints and deposit data into public repositories while hosting code on GitHub. The team includes investigators of biophysics alongside postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will receive training through organized hackathons.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: their material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, component exchange dynamics) arise from collective interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications, yet these properties cannot be predicted from single-molecule features alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), condensate-specific proteomic and interactome maps (CD-CODE, BioGRID, IntAct), structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting), and functional perturbation screens (CRISPR-based condensate disruption studies, disease-mutation databases like ClinVar and COSMIC). No integrated framework currently connects molecular grammar to emergent material properties to downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell imaging, and machine learning—to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and predictive modeling framework addressing a fundamental question: What combinatorial rules of sequence composition, structural motifs, PTMs, and interaction networks give rise to specific emergent material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally determine cellular outcomes such as transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, and signaling fidelity? 

The working group will first construct a harmonized meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across sequence/structural feature sets, experimentally measured or imaging-inferred material properties (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion kinetics, aspect ratios extracted from public microscopy datasets), and interactome/expression context. Using this resource, we will train interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings and disorder/PTM annotations) to predict emergent material properties from molecular features, explicitly testing whether scaling laws or phase diagrams generalize across protein families and cellular contexts. Second, we will cross-reference predicted material-property phenotypes with functional perturbation datasets (e.g., condensate-disrupting mutations linked to disease, optogenetic clustering screens) to test causal links between mesoscale material state and higher-order cellular function, addressing long-standing puzzles such as why chemically similar condensates (e.g., stress granules vs. P-bodies) exhibit distinct dynamics and functional consequences. 

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analysis, and cell biology, plus computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets. NCEMS support will enable dataset harmonization workshops, shared computational pipelines, and coordination across geographically distributed labs. All curated datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned community resource (FAIR-compliant), with tutorials and hackathon-style training events specifically designed to onboard graduate students and postdocs into data-intensive condensate biology, cultivating a new generation of researchers fluent in both wet-lab condensate biophysics and computational data synthesis.

title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Phenotype Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Initiative
title_norm: decoding the sequencetophenotype grammar of biomolecular condensate emergence a multiscale data synthesis initiative
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation involve interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins and nucleic acids, producing extensive but disconnected structural, kinetic, interactome, and single cell expression data. Despite abundant resources lacking standardization across independent databases, there is currently no integrated framework connecting sequence level molecular features and biophysical parameters to emergent cellular phenotypes and functional outcomes. To predict condensate material properties, evaluate disease mutations, and analyze evolutionary conservation, the project will synthesize multi scale datasets through feature engineering, natural language processing, gradient boosted trees, and physical models within containerized workflows. The research will integrate key databases including PhaSepDB, BioGRID, and ClinVar by mapping variables to a custom standardized ontology encompassing sequence features, biophysical parameters, and phenotypes structured within a relational database. This work will yield a reusable methodological framework for multi scale biological data integration that connects molecular sequence properties directly to macroscopic condensate behaviors and disease mechanisms.
full_text: This project investigates liquid liquid phase separation of intrinsically disordered proteins to connect molecular features with emergent cellular phenotypes. Extensive data exists regarding phase separating protein sequences and interactome networks but these resources remain disconnected and unstandardized. The proposed study integrates datasets to predict condensate properties and link molecular sequences directly with macroscopic disease mechanisms. The study design spans two years encompassing overlapping phases for data harmonization and feature engineering and subsequent model validation. Key methods include natural language processing and gradient boosted trees and graph neural networks alongside custom disorder aware sequence alignment. Model performance will undergo nested cross validation and subsequent testing against held out experimental datasets and external community benchmarks. The project will utilize numerous databases including UniProt and BioGRID alongside resources from the Human Protein Atlas and ClinVar. Distinct datasets will be integrated by mapping variables to a custom ontology within a relational database utilizing Bioschemas standards. The team will mitigate data heterogeneity and variations in experimental conditions by developing a unified ontology and utilizing mixed effects modeling. The two year timeline schedules data harmonization and feature engineering before concluding with hypothesis testing and final model validation. Integrating biological data across multiple scales necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration providing simultaneous expertise in polymer physics and computational network analysis. The team will share data and code publicly on Zenodo and GitHub with appropriate open source licenses and metadata. The cross disciplinary team includes principal investigators and postdoctoral researchers alongside graduate students receiving training through hackathons and joint mentorship.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic mesoscale emergent phenomenon, arising from multivalent, low-affinity interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct biophysical properties and cellular functions. Despite an explosion of data characterizing condensates across scales—from intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence features to interactome networks to live-cell imaging phenotypes—the field lacks an integrated framework connecting molecular grammar to cellular outcome. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets spanning five layers of biological organization: (1) sequence/structural databases of phase-separating proteins (PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CatGRANULE outputs); (2) proteome-wide interactome and post-translational modification data (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, STRING); (3) cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource); (4) single-molecule and FRAP kinetic measurements of condensate dynamics deposited in supplementary datasets across hundreds of published studies; and (5) single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data linking condensate-associated protein expression to cellular phenotypes and disease states (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, CCLE). No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, biophysical expertise, and cell biology domain knowledge required to harmonize these heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets—many collected with different assay conditions, buffer compositions, and imaging modalities—into a unified predictive model. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis challenge NCEMS is positioned to catalyze. Our working group will bring together biophysicists specializing in polymer theory of LLPS, structural biologists with cryo-EM/ET expertise, computational biologists skilled in graph-based interactome analysis, and cell biologists studying condensate function in stress response, transcription, and neurodegeneration. We will develop a standardized ontology and data harmonization pipeline (leveraging FAIR principles) to align sequence features, biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, surface tension), and phenotypic readouts into a unified multi-scale database. Using this integrated resource, we will apply machine learning and biophysical modeling to test three novel hypotheses: (i) whether condensate material properties (liquid vs. gel vs. solid) can be predicted from combinatorial sequence grammar and interactor stoichiometry; (ii) whether condensate emergence thresholds correlate with disease-associated mutations across cancer and neurodegeneration datasets; and (iii) whether evolutionary conservation patterns in IDRs predict condensate functional conservation across species. Deliverables include an open-access, versioned meta-database (deposited via Zenodo/GitHub with full analytical code), a generalizable predictive model of condensate emergence, and reproducible workflows adhering to community open-science standards. The project will directly train 4-6 graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, biophysical modeling, and open science practices through structured hackathons and co-mentorship across participating labs. By synthesizing molecular-scale sequence data with cellular-scale phenotypic outcomes, this working group will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how simple sequence and interaction rules generate the emergent complexity of condensate behavior—while establishing a template for future mesoscale synthesis research supported by NCEMS.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Emergent Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Framework Linking Sequence, Structure, and Cellular Phenotype
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of emergent biomolecular condensates a multiscale data synthesis framework linking sequence structure and cellular phenotype
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation possess immense biological importance regarding the relationship between molecular components and emergent mesoscale properties, yet existing datasets remain severely isolated across disciplines. The primary objective is to evaluate whether a molecular grammar predicts condensate phase separation and state transitions, applying an analytical strategy that will engineer features to train multi modal graph neural networks, transformer based sequence models, and biophysical algorithms. The project will integrate key datasets including PhaSepDB, DisProt, the Human Protein Atlas, and AlphaFold models by standardizing metadata schemas and encoding sequence and structural features into a unified protein interaction graph. This research will establish a computational framework for predicting mesoscale emergence, significantly advancing the understanding of how aberrant condensate phase transitions relate to severe diseases like neurodegeneration and cancer.
full_text: The domain of liquid liquid phase separation (LLPS) lacks understanding of how molecular features dictate properties of biomolecular condensates. Existing data on structural models and cellular expression remain isolated by discipline without connecting molecular sequences to mesoscale behaviors. The primary objective determines whether machine learning models can predict transitions of state linked to neurodegeneration and cancer. This two year project synthesizes five classes of public data to train machine learning models predicting properties of condensates. The core methods feature biophysical algorithms (CIDER) alongside multi modal graph neural networks and standard analyses of network enrichment. The team will validate these models using held out splits of data and benchmark them against published experimental results. The project incorporates public databases like PhaSepDB and DisProt alongside structural models from AlphaFold and functional screening libraries. The team will integrate these diverse sources by encoding embeddings of structures into a unified representation of interactions. The proposed study resolves inconsistent nomenclature across existing datasets by developing standardized vocabularies and a unified schema for metadata. This two year timeline features four overlapping phases from initial harmonization of data through final development of predictive tools. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to synthesize disparate data types using expertise in polymer physics and machine learning. The team will share data via Zenodo and host open source code on GitHub alongside open access publications. The team integrates faculty and trainees from diverse biological disciplines to provide instruction in cross disciplinary workflows for computation.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), RNA, and multivalent interactions generate organelle-like structures with functions not predictable from individual molecular components alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, structural biology datasets, single-cell spatial atlases, and functional genomic screens exist in isolation, preventing a unified understanding of how molecular grammar dictates emergent mesoscale organization and downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning—to integrate five classes of publicly available data: (1) curated LLPS driver/scaffold databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro) and disorder annotations (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) structural and interaction data from the PDB, EMDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted structures, including cryo-ET tomograms of native condensates; (3) single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens) capturing condensate-associated protein expression across cell states; (4) high-throughput perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR screens, ORFeome overexpression libraries) linking condensate-associated genes to cellular phenotypes; and (5) live-cell imaging repositories (e.g., OpenCell, LLPSDB) documenting condensate dynamics, material properties, and stress responses. No single dataset or lab possesses the breadth needed to bridge molecular sequence features to emergent mesoscale phase behavior and its physiological consequences—this synthesis requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, and network-based phenotype mapping. Our central hypothesis is that a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—combinations of valency, disorder patterning, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding motifs—predicts not only condensate formation propensity but also material state transitions (liquid-to-gel-to-solid) that underlie both normal cellular function and disease-associated aggregation. We will develop multi-modal graph neural network models trained on integrated sequence-structure-interaction data, validated against independent perturbation and imaging datasets, to predict emergent condensate properties and their causal links to cellular outcomes such as stress granule dynamics, transcriptional condensate function, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. The working group will produce: (i) an open, harmonized multi-omic condensate database with standardized ontologies, (ii) predictive models and interactive tools for the community, and (iii) a mechanistic framework connecting molecular-scale grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be released under FAIR and open-science principles via community repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase). The project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how simple molecular rules give rise to complex, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in living cells.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Cross-Species, Multi-Omics Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence and Its Cellular Consequences
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of biomolecular condensates a crossspecies multiomics synthesis of mesoscale emergence and its cellular consequences
abstract_text: The mesoscale emergence domain investigates biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation, where valuable datasets for phase behavior and clinical variants remain isolated by incompatible ontologies that prevent cross scale integration. Disconnected datasets leave a critical gap where no unified model connects the molecular sequence features of condensate forming proteins to mesoscale material properties and cellular scale phenotypic outcomes. The primary objective will determine quantitative rules connecting sequences to cellular phenotypes utilizing a four phase synthesis strategy that applies extract transform load pipelines, attention based models, and gradient boosted trees to map sequences to material states. The project will integrate databases including PhaSepDB, OpenCell, and ClinVar by building a unified relational and graph database schema that maps identifiers across sources and establishes a consensus material state ontology. A validated sequence to function model will predict pathological phase behavior from genetic data, explain evolutionary conservation patterns, and identify the mechanistic basis of disease associated mutations.
full_text: This project studies mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates and seeks unified models connecting molecular sequences to cellular phenotypes. Available datasets for phase behavior and clinical variants remain isolated and use incompatible ontologies that prevent cross scale integration. The study determines rules connecting sequences to condensate properties to enable prediction of pathological behavior from genetic data. The four phase strategy synthesizes data through harmonization and machine learning before validation of predictions against single cell datasets. The team applies extract transform load pipelines and gradient boosted trees alongside attention based models and sparse regression techniques. Results will undergo validation through nested cross validation and comparison against biophysical null models and held out perturbation datasets. The project extracts information from resources including PhaSepDB and OpenCell alongside the Human Cell Atlas and ClinVar databases. The researchers will integrate these sources by building a unified relational schema to map identifiers and establish consensus ontologies. The schema resolves incompatible units while stratified cross validation and independent test splits mitigate risks of overfitting and leakage. The two year timeline progresses from data harmonization to modeling of sequences before integration of variants and final validation. Processing large scale datasets requires cross disciplinary collaboration spanning biophysics and cell imaging alongside evolutionary genomics and structural biology. The project will publish open source code on GitHub and deposit harmonized data into repositories with persistent identifiers (DOIs). The team unites senior investigators with graduate students and visiting early career scholars from minority serving institutions for training.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation and related processes—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to functional subcellular compartments not predictable from any single molecule's properties. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive 'grammar' linking molecular-scale features (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalency, stoichiometry, post-translational modification patterns) to mesoscale material properties (droplet viscosity, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes (stress granule dynamics, transcriptional bursting, cell fate transitions). This gap persists because the necessary data are scattered across incompatible resources curated by disconnected communities: biophysicists studying in vitro phase diagrams, cell biologists generating high-content imaging atlases, proteomicists cataloging condensate constituents, evolutionary biologists tracking IDR conservation, and clinical genomicists annotating disease-associated mutations. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these disparate data types into a coherent cross-scale model. This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, computational structural biologists, cell imaging specialists, evolutionary genomicists, and clinical variant scientists to synthesize existing public datasets—including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB (condensate composition and phase behavior), OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization imaging), BioGRID/IntAct (interactomes), Human Cell Atlas and single-cell perturbation atlases (transcriptomic consequences across cell states), OrthoDB/Ensembl (cross-species IDR conservation), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (disease-linked mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Using this integrated dataset, we will: (1) train interpretable machine learning models that map sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features to empirically observed condensate material states and client recruitment specificity; (2) test whether evolutionary conservation patterns of IDR grammar predict functional robustness or tunability of condensate properties across orthologous proteins in diverse species; (3) determine whether disease-associated mutations in condensate scaffolds and clients cluster at predicted grammar 'hotspots' and whether this predicts pathological mesoscale-to-cellular phenotypic outcomes (e.g., aberrant stress granule persistence in neurodegeneration, altered chromatin condensate formation in cancer); and (4) build a generalizable cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular grammar to emergent cellular behavior, tested against independent public single-cell perturbation datasets. This synthesis is intractable for any individual lab given the scale of data harmonization, cross-domain expertise, and computational infrastructure required, and directly requires NCEMS support for data engineering, workshop convening, and shared analytical infrastructure. The Working Group will operate under FAIR and open-science principles, releasing all harmonized datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows via public repositories. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on each data-integration module, receiving structured training in multi-omics data science, biophysical modeling, and collaborative team science, while a rotating visiting-scholar program will recruit early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation. The project's central deliverable—a public, cross-species 'condensate grammar atlas'—will provide the field's first quantitative bridge between molecular sequence, mesoscale organization, and cellular emergent behavior.

The working group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computer science, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, FAIR data stewardship, and emergence-focused hypothesis generation. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open-source resource, establishing a reusable framework for mesoscale emergence research applicable beyond condensate biology to other multi-scale cellular phenomena.

abstract_text: Mesoscale cell biology investigates biomolecular condensates and liquid liquid phase separation, which requires computational integration across biological scales bridging in vitro sequence biophysics, cellular imaging, and systems biology network mapping. This Working Group proposes to synthesize five previously siloed classes of public data: (1) sequence-based IDR and low-complexity domain predictions (e.g., from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets); (2) curated condensate/LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) cataloguing experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their in vitro conditions; (3) genome-scale PPI and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD); (4) quantitative single-cell imaging and localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging, LLPSDB-linked microscopy) capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics; and (5) proteomic abundance and post-translational modification datasets (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) that modulate condensation propensity in vivo. By harmonizing these disparate data types—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance modalities—we will build predictive, mechanistic models of condensate emergence that no single dataset or disciplinary approach could achieve alone.

We will use graph neural networks and multi-modal representation learning to integrate these layers, testing whether emergent condensate properties (size, number, material state, responsiveness to stress) can be predicted from lower-scale features, and identifying network motifs or sequence grammars that generalize across protein families and cell types. Validation will leverage held-out experimental datasets and cross-species comparisons (yeast, human, plant) to test universality of discovered rules.

This project requires collaboration among condensate biophysicists, network biologists, imaging data scientists, and machine learning experts—expertise no single lab possesses collectively—and NCEMS support for compute infrastructure, data harmonization workshops, and cross-database ontology alignment. The Working Group will include graduate students and postdocs in hands-on data integration, model-building, and reproducible workflow design, producing open-source pipelines, harmonized datasets, and a public condensate-emergence prediction resource. All code, integrated datasets, and models will be released under FAIR and open-science standards, providing a template for mesoscale emergence research broadly.

This working group will integrate existing public datasets spanning scales from sequence to cell state. Data sources will include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification repositories, protein-RNA interaction maps, affinity and proximity interaction datasets, spatial proteomics, public live-cell imaging datasets, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate-associated biomolecules to physicochemical features, interaction topology, cell-type context, subcellular localization, perturbation outcomes, and reported material or dynamical properties.

To answer this, the project will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models that distinguish condensate classes and identify higher-order feature combinations not apparent from individual datasets. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone, such as multicomponent interaction density, RNA-dependent buffering, post-translational modification logic, and context-specific rewiring during stress, differentiation, or disease.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or infrastructure to synthesize the relevant public data types at community scale. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, network theorists, machine-learning researchers, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS workshops will enable consensus building around condensate ontologies, metadata standards, uncertainty scoring, benchmark datasets, and reproducible analytical workflows.

Expected outcomes include: an open condensate emergence knowledge graph; benchmark datasets for predicting mesoscale condensate behaviors; interpretable models identifying molecular and contextual rules of condensate formation and maturation; and community guidelines for integrating heterogeneous condensate data. The project will train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows through team-based data synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary short courses on open science, graph analytics, and AI-assisted biological discovery. All code, harmonized metadata, model outputs, tutorials, and manuscripts will be released publicly under open licenses.

By synthesizing diverse public data rather than generating new experiments, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do molecular-scale features collectively produce emergent mesoscale organization that shapes cellular behavior? The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

Despite thousands of studies, the field lacks a predictive synthesis explaining why the same protein can form a condensate in one cellular context but remain diffuse in another, or when condensate formation produces measurable cellular outcomes. We will build an open, cross-scale Condensate Emergence Atlas by harmonizing existing datasets that are currently siloed across disciplines. Cellular state and outcome layers will incorporate public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq and CRISPR screen datasets, DepMap dependencies, and disease-associated variant resources.

The project will develop reusable analytical strategies for emergence research. First, we will create controlled vocabularies and probabilistic labels for condensate presence, morphology, dynamics, and cellular context, explicitly representing uncertainty across datasets. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and graph-based models to connect molecular features, interaction networks, RNA context, post-translational modifications, and cell-state variables to observed mesoscale condensate formation. Third, we will test whether inferred condensate states explain higher-level cellular outcomes, such as stress survival, transcriptional rewiring, growth defects, and disease variant impact, beyond predictions from single-molecule properties alone. The central deliverable will be a set of open models that distinguish generalizable principles from dataset-specific artifacts and generate prioritized, experimentally testable hypotheses for the broader community.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the combined expertise or infrastructure to integrate image analysis, protein biophysics, RNA biology, cell biology, network science, functional genomics, and open-science software engineering at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, computational biophysicists, bioimage analysts, data curators, machine-learning researchers, cell-state and genomics experts, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working sessions will be used to establish shared data standards, perform collaborative model benchmarking, train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible synthesis workflows, and engage community stakeholders who maintain relevant public resources.

All products will follow open science principles: curated metadata, harmonized feature tables, analysis notebooks, containerized workflows, model code, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released publicly with clear documentation and community contribution mechanisms. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular sciences: how molecular-scale properties combine with cellular context to generate emergent mesoscale organization and cell-level consequences.

Despite thousands of public datasets on protein localization, phase separation, RNA binding, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation, a central question remains unresolved: what molecular and cellular contexts determine when condensates form, what material states they adopt, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build and test an integrative, predictive framework for condensate emergence across human cells and model organisms.

The project will assemble a community-scale team spanning molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure. The group will integrate existing public resources including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold and protein language model embeddings, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, public stress-response transcriptomics, CRISPR perturbation screens from DepMap and BioGRID ORCS, and ClinVar/gnomAD disease variant annotations. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize these heterogeneous datasets into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular state, mesoscale morphology, dynamics, and phenotypic outcomes.

The core scientific innovation is to treat condensates not merely as lists of phase-separating proteins, but as emergent systems whose properties depend on multivalent molecular grammar, expression stoichiometry, post-translational modification potential, RNA context, interaction network topology, and cellular stress history. We will develop transparent AI and statistical models to predict three linked outcomes: condensate membership, emergent material or morphological class, and downstream cellular consequence after perturbation. By comparing predictions across stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P bodies, nuclear speckles, and disease-associated aggregates, we will test whether shared rules govern distinct condensate systems or whether each represents a context-specific emergent regime. A special focus will be placed on long-standing puzzles, including why proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions produce different condensate behaviors, why some condensates are protective while others become pathological, and how disease mutations shift mesoscale organization without necessarily altering canonical molecular function.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis beyond the scope of any single laboratory: cross-dataset ontology alignment, image-derived feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate classes, and community governance for reusable data products. Working-group meetings will produce shared standards for condensate metadata, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and open tutorials. Trainees from diverse institutions will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams and trained in data integration, responsible AI, reproducible workflow design, and collaborative synthesis science.

All outputs will be released openly, including curated datasets, code, model cards, workflow containers, documentation, and interactive visualization tools. The expected outcome is a generalizable synthesis framework for predicting how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behavior and cellular phenotypes, providing a foundational resource for emergence-focused molecular and cellular biology.

title: A Public-Data Synthesis Atlas of Emergent Biomolecular Condensate States and Their Coupling to Cellular Phenotypes
title_norm: a publicdata synthesis atlas of emergent biomolecular condensate states and their coupling to cellular phenotypes
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions, and investigating their transitions between functional and dysfunctional states is critical to understand their varied cellular outcomes across diverse biological systems. This project will build a predictive atlas using public data by harmonizing datasets and applying graph neural networks, multimodal representation learning, and image extraction tools to determine how combined factors influence specific condensate states and cellular phenotypes. Data from resources including the Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting, and DisProt will be integrated by harmonizing metadata with standardized ontologies to construct a knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, images, perturbations, and phenotypes. The resulting predictive atlas will shift focus from cataloging components to identifying universal rules of emergent mesoscale states, enabling computational prediction of condensate behavior across different systems.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensates to identify the molecular and environmental factors driving their transitions into dysfunctional aggregates. These condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions but fragmented studies obscure the general rules governing their cellular outcomes. The proposed study asks how diverse factors dictate condensate states to uncover universal rules enabling broad computational predictions. The study design harmonizes existing public datasets into a unified framework for computational modeling of conserved condensate states. The analytical approach employs multimodal representation learning alongside graph neural networks (GNNs) and image extraction tools like CellProfiler. The predictive models require validation through benchmarking against held out datasets that span diverse organisms and cell types. The project utilizes diverse public databases including the Human Protein Atlas alongside specialized repositories such as OMIM and BioGRID. The team will harmonize metadata using standardized ontologies to construct a knowledge graph linking molecules and cellular phenotypes. The researchers will mitigate confirmation bias through curation of negative examples and bypass redistribution restrictions using accession links. The timeline spans 36 months and includes intermediate milestones for a prototype knowledge graph and robust predictive models. The expansive project scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to unite essential expertise in machine learning and cell biology. The team will release derived data and code under permissive licenses via public repositories including GitHub and Zenodo. The diverse group includes investigators from minority serving institutions alongside postdoctoral fellows gaining expertise in reproducible computational workflows.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions, yet their organizing principles remain difficult to generalize across cell types, stresses, and organisms. A central unresolved question is: which combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental perturbations cause condensates to transition from adaptive, dynamic assemblies to dysfunctional states that alter gene expression, signaling, or viability? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build a predictive, open atlas linking condensate composition, material properties, spatial organization, and cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing datasets from proteomics of stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated aggregates; fluorescence imaging and image-derived phenotypes from resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, and Image Data Resource; public perturbation data including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, LINCS, DepMap, and stress-response transcriptomics; and curated databases of intrinsically disordered regions, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding proteins, phase-separation assays, protein interaction networks, and disease variants. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into a common representation of condensate-associated mesoscale states. We will develop graph- and representation-learning approaches that combine molecular features, interaction topology, localization patterns, perturbation responses, and phenotypic readouts to identify recurrent ‘condensate state modules.’ These modules will be tested computationally for conservation across organisms, sensitivity to stress, enrichment for disease variants, and association with emergent cellular phenotypes such as translational repression, transcriptional bursting, DNA damage response, senescence, or toxicity. A key innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward identifying emergent state rules: for example, whether specific combinations of low-complexity sequence composition, RNA abundance, phosphorylation potential, network centrality, and local concentration predict reversible assembly versus persistent pathological aggregation. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, RNA biology, network science, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data resources, and computational biology groups, with structured roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in FAIR data curation, reproducible workflow design, cloud-based analysis, image feature extraction, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly accessible condensate-state knowledge graph, reusable analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate behavior, community-developed metadata standards for condensate-related public data, and a synthesis manuscript defining cross-system principles of condensate emergence. By transforming dispersed public datasets into a unified framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular biosciences: how collective mesoscale assemblies acquire properties not predictable from individual molecules alone, and how those emergent properties propagate upward to shape cellular physiology and disease.

title: Data-Synthesis Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence Across Cell Types, Perturbations, and Disease States
title_norm: datasynthesis atlas of biomolecular condensate emergence across cell types perturbations and disease states
abstract_text: Within mesoscale cellular biology, biomolecular condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions to regulate essential cellular processes, making the understanding of their formation and function vital for the field. This project will synthesize public data to identify general rules of emergent condensate behaviors using sequential metadata harmonization, graph based data integration, and diverse machine learning methods including weakly supervised computer vision, graph neural networks, and contrastive representation learning. Standardized metadata from repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, ENCODE, and AlphaFold will be mapped into a heterogeneous knowledge graph linking molecules, condensates, cellular contexts, biological perturbations, images, and phenotypes. This research will produce a predictive framework linking physical condensate properties to specific cellular phenotypes, thereby transitioning the field from isolated descriptive catalogs toward generalized rules of disease vulnerabilities.
full_text: This project examines mesoscale cellular biology to determine how molecular features and cellular contexts form functional condensates and disease associated assemblies. Condensates regulate cellular processes through multivalent interactions but fragmented data from isolated cases obscure the general principles of their emergence. The goal is to synthesize public datasets into a predictive framework that connects physical properties of condensates with cellular phenotypes. This computational synthesis of public data combines metadata harmonization and machine learning to construct a predictive atlas of molecular features. The analytical methods incorporate weakly supervised computer vision and graph neural networks alongside contrastive representation learning and Bayesian hierarchical models. Results will be validated using nested cross validation and the testing of external datasets alongside ablation analyses and permutation controls. The researchers will utilize datasets from the Human Protein Atlas and BioImage Archive alongside protein databases like AlphaFold and UniProt. The project will integrate data by mapping standardized metadata into a heterogeneous knowledge graph that connects molecules with cellular phenotypes. Known data limitations include batch effects and incomplete labels that require mitigation through controlled vocabularies and strict grading of evidence. The two year timeline delivers a prototype atlas at month nine and concludes with a public release at month 24. The synthesis of diverse data from omics and imaging demands cross disciplinary collaboration across biology and computer science beyond one laboratory. The team will release all harmonized datasets and code publicly under permissive licenses while adhering to established FAIR principles. The cross disciplinary team unites cell biologists and machine learning researchers from diverse institutions to provide substantial mentoring opportunities for trainees.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale phenomenon: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions, yet display emergent properties such as selective partitioning, viscoelasticity, spatial organization, and regulatory influence on transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and cellular contexts determine when condensates form adaptive regulatory hubs versus pathological or dysfunctional assemblies? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and perturbational data to build an open, cross-scale atlas linking condensate composition and physicochemical features to cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease states.

The project will integrate existing datasets from public repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting and fluorescence microscopy datasets, PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics studies, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic and chromatin datasets, DepMap and CRISPR perturbation screens, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural models, and published condensate interactomes. We will harmonize heterogeneous data describing protein localization, intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA-binding capacity, expression stoichiometry, interaction networks, and perturbation phenotypes. Using graph-based data integration, weakly supervised computer vision, representation learning, and interpretable machine learning, we will identify combinations of molecular features and environmental conditions that predict emergent condensate behaviors such as stress-induced assembly, nucleolar or nuclear body reorganization, granule persistence, and links to phenotypes including growth, differentiation, viral response, neurodegeneration, and cancer vulnerability.

The core scientific goal is to move beyond single-condensate case studies toward general principles of mesoscale emergence. We will test three synthesis questions: (1) Are there conserved molecular “design rules” that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated assemblies? (2) How do changes in expression, modification state, and interaction-network topology combine nonlinearly to produce condensate formation or dissolution? (3) Can condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from individual protein abundance or interaction data alone? The resulting models will generate community-testable hypotheses, such as specific combinations of low-complexity domains, RNA availability, phosphorylation sites, and network position that confer context-dependent condensate behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, standardize, and analyze the breadth of imaging, proteomic, structural, genomic, and perturbation data needed to infer general principles of condensate emergence. The working group will assemble cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, data curators, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, and trainees from research-intensive, primarily undergraduate, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS working group meetings will enable consensus development on metadata standards, benchmark tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable modeling strategies.

All products will follow open science principles: harmonized datasets, code, model weights, workflows, documentation, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories with reproducible containers and community governance. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary analysis sprints, receive training in FAIR data stewardship, image analysis, network science, and responsible AI, and co-lead open tutorials for the broader community. By synthesizing existing public data at community scale, this project will provide a predictive framework for how molecular features give rise to emergent mesoscale condensate states and how those states shape cellular function.

abstract_text: The domain of mesoscale emergence investigates membraneless biomolecular condensates, which are crucial structures that regulate cellular processes through multivalent weak interactions, intrinsically disordered regions, nucleic acid scaffolds, and post translational modifications. Despite extensive multi omics and imaging datasets, these resources remain disconnected, preventing systematic prediction of why certain condensates form adaptive assemblies while others transition into pathological states. This project will determine which combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts predict emergent condensate states by extracting microscopy phenotypes via computer vision and training interpretable multimodal graph neural networks. The research will integrate diverse databases, including UniProt, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas, into a unified knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, and imaging phenotypes via mapped community ontologies. This framework will computationally predict emergent cellular organization, enabling the interpretation of disease variants and the generation of specific perturbation hypotheses based on context dependent assembly rules.
full_text: This project explores mesoscale emergence of membraneless condensates (stress granules) to understand why adaptive assemblies transition into pathological states. Multivalent weak interactions drive these condensates but extensive molecular data lack integration to connect specific features with mesoscale phenotypes. The study determines which molecular combinations predict emergent condensate states and subsequently enables computational interpretation of variants associated with disease. The study design features secondary analysis of public data to construct a knowledge graph and train multimodal computational models. The team applies graph neural networks and foundation models for microscopy through containerized environments and dedicated workflow managers. The researchers validate results through nested cross validation and benchmark performance against negative controls of non condensate proteins. A unified knowledge graph integrates these datasets to connect molecular components and cellular outcomes with phenotypes from imaging. The team mitigates incompatible data repositories and batch effects through specific sensitivity analyses and harmonization of imaging channels. The project spans 24 months and delivers an initial knowledge graph before culminating in a final integrated resource. Harmonizing these diverse data types requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite specialized expertise in molecular biophysics and machine learning. The researchers will release code and data under permissive licenses through public platforms like GitHub to ensure reproducibility. The diverse team spans multiple career stages and offers mentored leadership roles through virtual sprints and trainee exchanges.

Membraneless biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA damage foci exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, chromatin, metabolites, and post-translational modifications produce collective material states that regulate cellular physiology. Despite intense study, a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do some condensates form adaptive, reversible mesoscale assemblies whereas others transition into pathological or dysfunctional states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to develop a predictive, publicly available framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease contexts.

This Working Group will integrate existing public data spanning complementary modalities: protein and RNA sequence features; intrinsically disordered region annotations; post-translational modification databases; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction resources; proximity labeling datasets; CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens; single-cell and bulk transcriptomics; proteomics; live-cell and fixed-cell imaging repositories; and curated disease mutation databases. Rather than generating new experimental data, the project will harmonize and reanalyze these resources to ask: which combinations of molecular grammar, interaction network topology, expression context, and environmental perturbation are sufficient to predict condensate assembly, dissolution, localization, material maturation, and cellular consequences?

The analytical strategy will combine expertise from molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, image analysis, machine learning, network science, and open-source software engineering. We will first create an interoperable condensate knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, interaction evidence, perturbations, imaging-derived phenotypes, and cellular outcomes using transparent provenance standards. Second, we will develop reusable computer vision workflows to extract mesoscale condensate phenotypes from public microscopy data, including size distributions, number, spatial organization, coalescence signatures, and temporal reversibility where time-lapse data exist. Third, we will train interpretable multimodal AI models to identify predictive rules for condensate emergence and state transitions, explicitly testing whether conserved mesoscale behaviors can be inferred from molecular features across different biological contexts. Finally, we will perform cross-dataset validation using held-out perturbation and disease datasets to identify general principles and context-specific exceptions.

NCEMS support is essential because this synthesis exceeds the scope of a single laboratory: it requires coordinated data curation across many repositories, shared standards for condensate phenotypes, integration of heterogeneous molecular and imaging data, and sustained collaboration among experimentalists, computational scientists, statisticians, and trainees. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource communities, with explicit roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in data stewardship, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative team science.

All outputs will follow open science principles. We will release curated datasets, ontologies, analysis notebooks, trained models, image-analysis pipelines, and benchmark tasks through public repositories with documented metadata and community governance. The project will also produce training modules on multimodal biological data synthesis, interpretable AI, and reproducible mesoscale cell biology. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent predictive resource, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular properties generate emergent condensate states and how those states influence cellular adaptation, dysfunction, and disease.

full_text: This molecular and cellular biology project addresses the inability to predict mesoscale properties and phenotypic effects of biomolecular condensates. Weak multivalent interactions form cellular condensates but fragmented data obscures why similar molecules exhibit distinct assembly behaviors across contexts. The project investigates how molecular and cellular features dictate condensate participation to provide a predictive framework for disease variants. The study design synthesizes diverse public datasets into a knowledge graph to build nested predictive models of condensate formation. The analytical approach applies protein language models and graph neural networks alongside causal inference and physical feature engineering. The researchers will validate results using cross validation and temporal data splits alongside negative controls and feature ablation. The project relies on public databases including AlphaFold and UniProt alongside repositories like ENCODE and the BioImage Archive. The team will integrate these diverse resources into a versioned knowledge graph using persistent identifiers and standardized ontology terms. The researchers will mitigate data leakage and inherent biases by employing temporal data splits and publishing model cards. The two year timeline includes quarterly virtual meetings and in person synthesis workshops alongside trainee led analysis sprints. This cross disciplinary collaboration is required because integrating soft matter physics and machine learning exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The team will share all code and trained models publicly under open licenses using public repositories (including GitHub). The group includes biologists and machine learning researchers across multiple career stages who provide instruction in open science.
