abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions produce mesoscale assemblies with properties not predictable from individual components alone, including selective partitioning, altered reaction kinetics, and coordinated cellular responses. Despite rapid growth in condensate research, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when a protein or RNA will participate in condensates, what mesoscale state will emerge, and how that state influences cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: which molecular features and cellular contexts jointly determine emergent condensate behavior and downstream cell-state outcomes? We will integrate complementary public resources spanning molecular sequence, structure, localization, interaction, and phenotype. Data sources will include condensate and phase-separation databases, AlphaFold and Protein Data Bank structural models, UniProt and RNAcentral annotations, BioGRID and STRING interaction networks, OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets of stress granules and nuclear bodies, PRIDE proteomics, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic data, LINCS perturbational signatures, and genome-scale CRISPR or RNAi screens from DepMap and related repositories. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into an open, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features to mesoscale assemblies and phenotypic consequences. The working group will develop transparent analytical strategies combining computer vision, protein language models, graph machine learning, causal inference, and physical feature engineering. Image-based models will quantify condensate morphology, number, size distributions, coarsening, and spatial relationships across published microscopy datasets. Sequence and structure models will extract multivalency, disorder, charge patterning, interaction motifs, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites. Network and perturbation analyses will test whether emergent condensate states mediate cellular outcomes such as stress resistance, transcriptional repression, cell-cycle arrest, viral infection response, or cancer dependency. Rather than producing a black-box predictor alone, the group will compare mechanistic hypotheses: whether condensate emergence is best explained by intrinsic molecular grammar, cellular concentration and stoichiometry, interaction-network topology, post-translational regulation, or combinations of these factors. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or coordination capacity to integrate high-content imaging, proteomics, structural bioinformatics, RNA biology, soft-matter physics, machine learning, and causal modeling at community scale. The proposed team would include molecular and cell biologists studying condensates, computational biologists, biophysicists, statisticians, imaging scientists, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable consensus on metadata standards, benchmarking tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable model evaluation. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, trained models, and derived feature tables will be released under open licenses through reproducible containers and public repositories. Trainees will lead cross-institutional analysis modules, participate in data-integration hackathons, and receive training in open, team-based synthesis science. The expected outcomes are a reusable public atlas of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features, validated predictive models for emergent mesoscale organization, and testable hypotheses explaining how condensates convert molecular interactions into higher-order cellular phenotypes. By transforming fragmented public data into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental puzzle in cell biology and provide a community resource for predicting emergent organization across the molecular-to-cellular scale.

title_norm: a publicdata synthesis atlas of rules governing emergent biomolecular condensate states across human cell types
abstract_text: Within mesoscale cellular biology, human biomolecular condensates regulate critical processes like transcription and stress adaptation, though individual phase separation drivers like intrinsically disordered regions remain neither necessary nor sufficient in isolation. How nonlinear combinations of molecular features dictate protein behavior remains poorly understood, leaving a gap in generalized frameworks to predict functional condensate states and their cellular consequences. To test whether integrated multiscale public data predicts condensate formation more accurately than single modality approaches, this computational synthesis will harmonize features and develop models using multimodal deep learning and network propagation. The project will integrate datasets from UniProt, AlphaFold, OpenCell, and the Human Protein Atlas by mapping proteins to stable identifiers and combining structural, proteomic, and imaging features into a unified structure. This research will establish a reusable atlas to validate multimodal data integration, enabling standardized comparisons of condensates across varying cell types, molecular mechanisms, and disease contexts for downstream applications.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: thousands of weak molecular interactions can collectively produce spatially organized, dynamic compartments that alter signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, and stress responses without membrane boundaries. Yet a central unresolved question remains: when do molecular features such as intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA binding, and interaction-network topology combine to generate a condensate state with predictable cellular consequences? This working group will synthesize public molecular, imaging, proteomic, and functional genomics data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes.

We will integrate existing datasets from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, DepMap, BioGRID, STRING, UniProt, AlphaFold, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and publicly available single-cell transcriptomic and perturbation screens. The project will focus on human nuclear and cytoplasmic condensates involved in transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, DNA damage response, and stress adaptation. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will build a harmonized, open synthesis resource that connects protein sequence features, structural disorder, interaction valency, RNA association, post-translational modification, subcellular localization dynamics, cell-type context, and genetic dependency phenotypes.

The core scientific objective is to test whether condensate formation and functional impact can be predicted from multiscale public data better than from any individual data modality. We will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models to identify combinations of molecular features that distinguish constitutive condensate scaffolds, context-dependent clients, and disease-sensitive regulatory nodes. We will then ask how these mesoscale states map onto higher-order outcomes, including transcriptional programs, proliferation dependencies, stress resistance, and mutation-associated disease phenotypes. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that are not obvious from single-protein annotations, such as cooperative recruitment thresholds, modification-sensitive phase switching, and cell-type-specific condensate rewiring.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, computational imaging, graph theory, machine learning, RNA biology, structural bioinformatics, and open-science software engineering. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource teams, with intentional participation by early-career scientists, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows. NCEMS convening infrastructure will enable sustained cross-disciplinary synthesis, community standards for condensate data annotation, and collaborative benchmarking of computational models.

Deliverables will include an open Condensate Emergence Atlas; reproducible workflows for data harmonization, image-derived localization feature extraction, and multimodal modeling; benchmark datasets for predicting condensate membership and context-dependent function; and community-authored guidelines for integrating condensate-related public data. Trainees will participate in hackathons, model-building sprints, and team-science workshops focused on reproducible analysis, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent mesoscale synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular organization and function?

abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular biology, weak multivalent interactions drive the mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates, creating essential membraneless compartments that span a continuum from liquid to solid material states. The field lacks rules explaining what dictates condensate composition and pathological transitions because existing biophysical, proteomic, and genetic data remain highly fragmented across biased and unintegrated databases. This data synthesis project will determine how specific molecular features and interaction network architectures produce condensate material properties and downstream cellular outcomes by applying network science, causal discovery, and interpretable machine learning. The approach will construct a comprehensive knowledge graph utilizing community ontologies to integrate entities and metadata across phase separation databases like PhaSepDB, structural resources including AlphaFold, and diverse single cell atlases. This unified framework will transition the field from descriptive studies to predictive principles, resolving current debates regarding the precise molecular determinants of condensate specificity and pathological maturation.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale feature of cellular organization, yet the field lacks generalizable rules explaining why some molecular assemblies become dynamic functional compartments while others transition toward persistent aggregates or disease-associated states. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, genetic, and phenotypic datasets to answer a central question in emergence biology: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and network architecture give rise to condensates with distinct material properties and downstream cellular outcomes? The project will not generate new experimental data. Instead, it will integrate existing resources including LLPS and condensate databases, protein sequence and intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification datasets, protein interaction networks, public affinity-purification and proximity-labeling proteomics, microscopy image repositories, CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, and disease-variant databases. By linking molecular composition to mesoscale condensate behavior and cell-level phenotypes, the project will directly address NCEMS priorities in understanding emergent properties between biomolecules and organelles. The Working Group will develop an open, extensible Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph connecting proteins, RNAs, modifications, interaction motifs, environmental conditions, localization patterns, condensate classes, and phenotypic consequences. This resource will support three analytical aims. First, we will identify conserved and context-specific molecular signatures that predict condensate formation across cell types and organisms, distinguishing drivers, clients, and regulators. Second, we will infer how multivalent interactions, disorder, RNA binding, charge patterning, and post-translational modification jointly shape emergent material states such as liquid-like dynamics, gelation, and solidification. Third, we will connect condensate state transitions to higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress response, transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, signaling, and neurodegenerative disease phenotypes. Methodologically, the team will combine network science, interpretable machine learning, causal discovery, natural-language mining of the literature, and computer vision applied to public microscopy images. A major innovation will be the development of benchmark datasets and transparent models that predict condensate behavior from molecular and contextual features while quantifying uncertainty and dataset bias. This synthesis effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the expertise or coordination capacity to harmonize heterogeneous public datasets spanning biophysics, cell biology, genomics, proteomics, imaging, and clinical genetics. The Working Group will include condensate biologists, protein biophysicists, RNA biologists, data scientists, image analysts, network theorists, and experts in open scientific software from diverse institutions and career stages. Trainees will participate through structured data-synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow workshops, cross-lab mentoring, and leadership roles in benchmark construction and software documentation. All products will follow open science principles: curated datasets, metadata standards, code, workflows, model outputs, and tutorials will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers and community governance. The expected outcome is a predictive, community-validated framework for explaining how molecular-scale features generate mesoscale condensate properties and how those properties influence cellular function. This will transform a fragmented literature into a reusable synthesis platform, resolve long-standing debates about determinants of condensate specificity and pathological maturation, and train a new cohort of scientists in collaborative, data-intensive molecular and cellular biology.

abstract_original:
Membraneless organelles formed by biomolecular condensation exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites produce dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, biochemical activities, and cellular consequences. Yet a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and environmental contexts determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, biophysical, and phenotypic datasets to derive generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes. The project will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies involving proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, and DDX family helicases.

The effort will integrate existing data from public repositories including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, ENCODE, DepMap, and disease variant resources such as ClinVar and gnomAD. We will harmonize heterogeneous data types spanning protein sequence features, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding properties, interaction networks, in vitro phase-separation measurements, live-cell condensate imaging, FRAP-derived dynamics, perturbational transcriptomics, proteomics, genetic dependency profiles, and disease-associated mutations. No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. By transforming fragmented public data into testable rules of mesoscale organization, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how collective molecular interactions generate emergent compartments that shape cell fate.

Image foundation models will extract condensate features such as number, size distribution, morphology, coarsening behavior, and localization from public microscopy. Graduate students and postdocs will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducible workflow workshops, FAIR data curation sprints, and mentored team-authored publications.

All harmonized metadata, code, workflows, trained models, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released openly under community-approved licenses using reproducible containers and version-controlled repositories. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive synthesis of condensate emergence, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale cellular organization and higher-order cellular phenotypes.

Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions and reorganize cellular biochemistry without membrane boundaries. Although thousands of proteins and RNAs have been implicated in condensates, a central puzzle remains unresolved: when do condensates act as adaptive organizers that buffer cellular stress, and when do they become amplifiers of dysfunction leading to altered signaling, growth, or disease phenotypes? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, transcriptomic, and phenotypic datasets to identify generalizable principles linking condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes.

The project will use only existing public data, integrating resources such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold structures, post-translational modification repositories, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, ProteomeXchange stress-response proteomics, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, LINCS perturbational transcriptomics, DepMap fitness screens, and published high-content imaging screens. We will construct an open, versioned knowledge graph connecting condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction valency, post-translational modifications, localization, microscopy-derived condensate morphology, stress conditions, pathway activity, and cellular phenotypes. Using interpretable machine learning, network modeling, and causal-inference strategies, we will test whether specific combinations of molecular features and network positions predict emergent condensate behaviors such as nucleation, fusion, hardening, reversibility, recruitment selectivity, and downstream effects on transcription, translation, signaling, and cell viability.

The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate properties can be predicted from integrated molecular features and, in turn, whether those properties explain cellular-scale outcomes better than the properties of individual molecules alone. This directly addresses emergence across scales: local molecular interactions give rise to condensate material states, which then reshape information flow, biochemical reaction organization, and cellular decisions. The project will also resolve a long-standing inconsistency in the field by harmonizing heterogeneous condensate annotations, imaging measurements, and experimental contexts into a shared ontology that distinguishes evidence for phase separation, clustering, aggregation, and functional compartmentalization.

NCEMS support is essential because the work exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The Working Group will bring together condensate biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, bioimage analysts, data scientists, network theorists, ontology developers, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS will enable structured team science, dataset harmonization, cloud-based analysis, benchmark development, and community governance for open resources.

All outputs will follow open science principles: curated datasets, ontologies, code, workflows, trained models, documentation, and interactive visualization tools will be released publicly with reproducible computational environments. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary synthesis sprints, receive training in FAIR data practices, bioimage analysis, graph machine learning, and responsible AI, and co-lead benchmark challenges. The expected outcome is a community resource and predictive framework that transforms condensate biology from a catalog of components into a mechanistic, data-driven understanding of how mesoscale assemblies generate emergent cellular functions.

Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from weak multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet their cellular consequences remain difficult to predict: under what conditions do condensates buffer perturbations, amplify stress signals, sequester regulatory factors, or drive pathological transitions? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and phenotypic data to identify generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to cellular stress responses and fate decisions. The central hypothesis is that condensate function is not encoded by individual components alone, but emerges from network-level features such as interaction valency, compositional diversity, RNA coupling, post-translational modification state, and subcellular context. Testing this hypothesis requires integration across data types and expertise beyond any single laboratory.

We will build an open, harmonized condensate-to-phenotype atlas by integrating existing datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, PRIDE, GEO, SRA, LINCS, DepMap, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, BioGRID, IntAct, POSTAR, ENCODE, and curated phase-separation resources such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS. The atlas will link condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction networks, post-translational modifications, localization dynamics, microscopy-derived mesoscale properties, perturbation responses, and cellular phenotypes under stress conditions including heat shock, oxidative stress, nutrient limitation, viral infection, and DNA damage. No new experimental data will be generated.

The working group will address three questions. First, which molecular features best predict emergent condensate behaviors such as fusion, dissolution, hardening, spatial relocalization, and selective recruitment? Second, when do condensates act as robust buffers versus switch-like amplifiers of stress-response pathways? Third, can conserved mesoscale organizational principles explain why similar molecular components produce divergent outcomes across cell types, organisms, and perturbations? To answer these questions, we will combine computer vision, protein biophysics, RNA biology, network science, causal inference, and interpretable machine learning. Analytical products will include standardized image-derived condensate descriptors, a cross-dataset knowledge graph, benchmark prediction tasks, and multiscale models that relate molecular interaction features to cellular outcomes.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated community-scale curation, common data standards, shared computational infrastructure, and iterative synthesis among specialists who rarely work together: cell biologists studying stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and DNA repair foci; biophysicists modeling phase transitions; data scientists developing multimodal foundation models; statisticians focused on causal inference; and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. The working group will hold synthesis sprints, open code reviews, trainee-led benchmarking challenges, and cross-training modules in reproducible workflows, microscopy metadata standards, and responsible AI for molecular and cellular biology.

All outputs will follow open science principles. Curated datasets, metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, model code, benchmark results, and visualization tools will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers and community documentation. The project will provide a reusable framework for synthesizing heterogeneous data on mesoscale cellular organization, while producing testable principles for how emergent condensate properties shape higher-order cellular behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into predictive, interpretable models, this working group will help resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: how dynamic molecular assemblies acquire system-level functions that cannot be inferred from their individual components alone.

abstract_original: Membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles are archetypal mesoscale systems: they emerge from many weak molecular interactions yet shape translation, RNA fate, signaling, and cell survival. Despite extensive public data, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework explaining when specific RNAs and proteins form condensates, how condensate composition varies across cellular contexts, and which mesoscale properties causally associate with downstream cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize existing public datasets to answer a central question: what molecular, biophysical, and network features predict the emergent assembly, composition, dynamics, and cellular consequences of human RNP condensates? The project will integrate only publicly available data, including fluorescence imaging datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer, and published live-cell stress-granule studies; proteomic and interactome data from BioGRID, IntAct, AP-MS, proximity-labeling, and condensate-enrichment studies; RNA localization and RNA-protein interaction data from ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIP-seq, APEX-seq, and subcellular fractionation studies; perturbation and phenotype data from DepMap, genome-scale CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, and drug-response repositories; and sequence-derived features such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, prion-like domains, charge patterning, RNA-binding motifs, post-translational modification sites, and predicted structures. All outputs will be open: curated datasets, metadata standards, analysis notebooks, trained models, uncertainty estimates, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories. The expected outcome is a reusable predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in RNP condensates, providing testable hypotheses for the broader community and a model for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biology.

These dynamic assemblies bridge the critical gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, orchestrating essential cellular functions ranging from gene regulation to stress response. However, despite an exponential increase in individual laboratory studies, the universal biophysical rules and stoichiometric conditions that dictate the unexpected emergence of these mesoscale structures remain a long-standing mystery. Furthermore, predicting how localized condensate dynamics influence global, higher-order cellular outcomes remains beyond current capabilities. This gap in knowledge persists largely because existing experimental data—ranging from atomic-resolution structural biophysics to whole-cell spatial transcriptomics and high-content imaging—are highly siloed across disparate public repositories.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group" (MCS-WG), a transdisciplinary collaborative initiative designed to synthesize existing multimodal public datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By integrating fragmented data from PRIDE (mass spectrometry proteomics), GEO (transcriptomics), PhaSepDB (phase separation curation), AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (structural conformations), and the Image Data Resource (high-content cellular microscopy), our team will construct a massive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph. Crucially, this project will rely entirely on publicly available data, generating no new experimental data, thereby directly answering the NCEMS call for community-scale synthesis.

Our working group will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks, to identify hidden patterns that drive mesoscale phase separation. Our research objectives are threefold: (1) Answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation of disordered protein regions and their emergent phase-separation behaviors across distinct cellular stress states; (2) Solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly and disassembly; and (3) Develop an innovative, open-source AI analytical framework that predicts subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on molecular-level perturbations.

The complexity of this synthesis requires the unique support and resources of NCEMS, as it extends far beyond the computational or domain expertise of any single laboratory. The MCS-WG will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and machine learning experts from varied geographic locations and institutional tiers. In strong alignment with NCEMS goals, our initiative places a heavy emphasis on workforce development. We will actively recruit and cross-train early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) from historically underrepresented backgrounds, equipping them with a dual skill set in molecular biology and advanced data science. Furthermore, committing strictly to open science principles, all curated datasets, harmonized ontologies, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly via open-access community portals, ensuring reproducibility and providing a lasting resource for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will unravel how mesoscale emergence dictates cellular fate.

A unified framework is currently absent because public datasets remain isolated across biological scales, yielding a fragmented understanding of how nanoscale molecular interactions drive mesoscale condensate properties. The project will integrate resources including UniProt, DisProt, LLPSDB, and spatial transcriptomic atlases into a cloud based repository, structuring this information as a knowledge graph defining individual protein interaction probabilities. This work will deliver a unified predictive framework for liquid liquid phase separation, which could identify novel therapeutic targets for complex diseases involving abnormal phase transitions.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting example of emergent mesoscale organization. These membraneless compartments organize biochemical reactions dynamically, yet bridging the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and their mesoscale architectural properties remains a critical challenge. While abundant public data exist detailing the sequence characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and the cellular phenotypes of their dysregulation, a unified framework mapping this cross-scale emergence is absent. Currently, critical datasets—such as sequence features (UniProt, DisProt), structural predictions (AlphaFold), in vitro phase behaviors (LLPSDB, PhaSePro), mesoscale cellular imaging (Image Data Resource), and high-throughput phenotypic screens (DepMap)—remain highly siloed. No individual research laboratory possesses the combined expertise in molecular biophysics, spatial transcriptomics, artificial intelligence, and cellular biology necessary to bridge these data islands. To address this compelling scientific puzzle, we propose the 'Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC)' Working Group. This highly collaborative, transdisciplinary team will synthesize entirely publicly available datasets to decipher the rules governing emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. We will employ advanced AI and data science methodologies, specifically developing multimodal graph neural networks, to seamlessly integrate cross-scale data. The project is structured around three core synthesis objectives: (1) Map the molecular grammar of IDPs and associated post-translational modifications to mesoscale emergent properties such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration thresholds, and multiphase spatial architecture; (2) Link these emergent mesoscale features directly to cellular-level outcomes, specifically focusing on stress granule dynamics and neurodegenerative protein aggregation pathways; and (3) Develop open-source predictive algorithms capable of inferring higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences and available interactome topologies. This initiative goes far beyond the capabilities of an individual lab, necessitating the centralized support of NCEMS to unite diverse experts across geographic locations, institutional research levels, and career stages. The MCC Working Group will recruit diverse computational and biological scientists, intentionally embedding postdoctoral researchers and graduate students into the core data science workflows. This will provide unprecedented training opportunities, actively cultivating a data-savvy, next-generation workforce fluent in cross-disciplinary AI and biological synthesis. Furthermore, our initiative commits rigorously to community-created open science policies. We will release all harmonized multi-scalar datasets, machine learning models, and reproducible analysis pipelines via public GitHub repositories and a dedicated web portal, ensuring long-term utility for the molecular biosciences community. By decoding how simple molecular inputs trigger complex, non-linear mesoscale emergence, this synthesis project will answer long-standing mysteries regarding biological phase transitions, ultimately pioneering innovative analytical strategies for understanding cellular organization in health and disease.

Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of biomolecules spontaneously give rise to highly organized, functional, membrane-less organelles. These mesoscale structures dictate critical subcellular outcomes, ranging from stress adaptation to gene regulation. However, the precise rules governing how molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA secondary structures, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—dynamically scale to produce emergent mesoscale physical properties remain a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and spatial imaging datasets, these rich resources remain deeply siloed across disparate repositories. Addressing this complex emergent phenomenon requires a community-scale data synthesis approach that far exceeds the computational and disciplinary capabilities of any individual research laboratory.

We propose the establishment of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group to decode the multiscale grammar of condensate formation. This transdisciplinary team will unite domain experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, cell biology, and multi-omics. Adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate, we will generate no new experimental data. Instead, we will synthesize massive public datasets, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), and mesoscale spatial imaging (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). 

Our primary scientific objective is to develop an innovative, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework to uncover the hidden principles of mesoscale emergence. We will address a novel question: How do heterogeneous molecular inputs synergistically trigger the spatiotemporal emergence of specific condensates, such as stress granules, under shifting environmental pressures? By harmonizing these disparate, multi-scale data streams into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph, our AI-driven analytical strategy will predict how distinct molecular perturbations cascade upward to alter mesoscale properties—such as condensate size, viscosity, and composition—and ultimately influence cellular phenotypes.

Executing this transdisciplinary integration fundamentally relies on the unique infrastructure, computational resources, and collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives across career stages and institutional levels, we will translate fragmented biological data into a cohesive understanding of subcellular emergence. 

Crucially, the CES Working Group will adhere strictly to community-created open science policies. All integrated databases, AI models, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be distributed through open-source repositories following FAIR principles. Furthermore, this initiative will provide unparalleled training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through intensive, cross-disciplinary co-mentorship in advanced data science and systems biology, we will empower the future data-savvy workforce required to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.

Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and nucleoli, represent a quintessential example of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Arising from the dynamic, multivalent interactions of proteins and RNA, these membraneless organelles bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular functions. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress adaptation, and disease pathogenesis, the fundamental rules dictating how physical interactions at the atomic and molecular levels scale up to govern mesoscale condensation and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Current biological research often captures these phenomena in isolated silos—producing disparate datasets on molecular structure, pairwise protein-protein interactions, or cellular imaging—leaving a critical knowledge gap in bridging these temporal and spatial dimensions.

To address this fundamental question of emergence, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of publicly available biological data to decode the mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates. We will systematically integrate structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PDB), high-throughput interaction and proximity labeling networks (BioGRID, IntAct, PRIDE), transcriptomic profiles under distinct cellular stress states (GEO, SRA), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Our primary objective is to construct 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a predictive foundation model that mathematically maps how molecular grammars (such as intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, and interaction valencies) dictate emergent mesoscale properties (including droplet formation, material state transitions, and biochemical partitioning) and their subsequent cellular outcomes like gene regulation and stress survival.

It necessitates the specialized resources, computational infrastructure, and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team encompassing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and data ontologists. This diverse partnership deliberately bridges multiple geographic locations, career stages, and institutional types to ensure a breadth of scientific perspectives.

Through dedicated hackathons and cross-disciplinary mentorship, graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be cross-trained at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence and mesoscale biology. Strictly leveraging existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental datasets, this project will integrate sequence and structural databases (e.g., DisProt, AlphaFold DB), biophysical phase separation repositories (e.g., PhaSePro, CD-CODE), massive-scale stress-response proteomics (PRIDE, BioGRID), and high-resolution microscopy datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR).

Specifically, we will utilize multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and spatio-temporal deep learning to build predictive models. These models will map the continuum from molecular-level features (e.g., intrinsic disorder, valency) to mesoscale emergent properties (e.g., condensate viscosity, complex assembly/disassembly kinetics) and ultimately to cellular phenotypic outcomes, such as cellular resilience to environmental stress. 

This initiative heavily relies on the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. The CESA Working Group will convene a diverse assembly of experts, including molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, computational biologists, and AI/ML engineers. Our team is strategically assembled to reflect a broad spectrum of career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels (including primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions), ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

A cornerstone of our proposal is the rigorous training of the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees embedded within the Working Group will undergo intensive cross-training at the intersection of molecular cell biology and advanced computational data synthesis, gaining essential, highly translatable skills in AI-driven biology.

Adhering strictly to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, analytical workflows, and educational materials will be made publicly accessible via FAIR-compliant repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) and disseminated through an interactive, community-facing web portal. By synthesizing disparate public data to map the continuous trajectory from molecular biophysics to emergent mesoscale architecture, the CESA Working Group will solve critical mysteries of cellular emergence, provide the community with transformative open-source analytical tools, and establish a new paradigm for transdisciplinary discovery in the biosciences.

These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble from interacting networks of proteins and nucleic acids, fundamentally bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and complex subcellular organization. Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in biology. These dynamic, non-membrane-bound organelles assemble from individual macromolecules to exhibit entirely new collective properties—such as tunable viscosity, selective permeability, and spatially restricted biochemical reactions. They effectively bridge the gap between single biomolecules and higher-order cellular phenotypes. Despite an explosion of single-lab experimental studies, the universal sequence grammar, biophysical parameters, and thermodynamic thresholds governing this mesoscale emergence across space and time remain a long-standing puzzle. Furthermore, predicting how these mesoscale properties dictate macro-cellular behaviors, such as survival mechanisms during cellular stress, is currently beyond the computational and analytical capacity of any individual research group.

To address this critical gap, we propose the Working Group 'Condensome-AI', a transdisciplinary team comprising structural biologists, biophysicists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists. We will leverage artificial intelligence and advanced data science methodologies to synthesize massive, publicly available, yet currently siloed datasets. Specifically, we will integrate biophysical droplet databases (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, PDB), global interactome datasets (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-throughput cellular imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource). In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will generate no new experimental data. Instead, it relies entirely on community-scale synthesis to construct a unified, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence.

Our project pursues three core scientific objectives: (1) Answer the novel question of how combinations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and structured RNA-binding domains synergize to govern emergent rheological properties across different metabolic states; (2) Solve the long-standing mystery of how shifts in environmental energy and molecular composition trigger the sudden spatial and temporal appearance of these mesoscale structures; and (3) Develop 'MesoPredict,' an innovative, AI-driven analytical pipeline utilizing graph neural networks to predict condensate composition and subsequent cellular impacts directly from omics profiles.

Executing this synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative support of NCEMS. By bringing together diverse talent from distinct geographic locations and institutional tiers, we will foster a research environment impossible within traditional single-discipline grants. Our partnership emphasizes diversity and mentorship, deliberately pairing senior computational scientists with biology-focused graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through specialized computational bootcamps and collaborative working group sessions, we will actively train a data-savvy, next-generation workforce capable of navigating the intersection of AI and biological emergence.

Finally, our Working Group is deeply committed to rigorous open science practices. All synthesized datasets, AI/ML models, analytical workflows, and resultant code will be heavily documented, open-source, and distributed via community repositories like Zenodo and GitHub following FAIR data principles. By deciphering the complex language of mesoscale condensate emergence, this NCEMS-supported synthesis will fundamentally advance our understanding of cellular organization and provide a transformative, accessible resource for the entire molecular and cellular biosciences community.

Bridging the critical gap between individual macromolecules and complex cellular organelles, these membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. Individual research laboratories lack the cross-disciplinary expertise and computational infrastructure required to unify these divergent streams into a cohesive, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. Our working group will pursue three primary objectives: (1) Unify and harmonize these highly heterogeneous datasets to construct the first multi-scale Condensate Graph, mathematically representing the relationships between sequence-level features and mesoscale assembly. (2) Develop and train novel geometric deep learning models to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties—such as condensate liquidity, valency, and viscoelasticity—directly from these synthesized omics and structural data. (3) Map these mesoscale phase behaviors to higher-order subcellular and phenotypic outcomes, specifically focusing on how the dysregulation of this emergent grammar correlates with known disease markers. This endeavor directly aligns with the core mission of NCEMS. The sheer scale and complexity of bridging atomistic biophysics with cellular phenomics via machine learning necessitate a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research group. Our proposed Working Group deliberately brings together experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, structural biology, and spatial multi-omics from geographically diverse institutions and varying career stages. Central to our proposal is a steadfast commitment to workforce development and Open Science. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated as core analysts, receiving cross-training in AI-driven omics integration, biophysical modeling, and rigorous reproducible data science practices. Furthermore, in strict adherence to community-created open science policies, all integrated databases, machine learning codebases, and analytical workflows will be released publicly under FAIR principles. Ultimately, this data synthesis will solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful new computational lens to understand subcellular organization.

This project will determine if time of day influences the thermal sensitivity of trafficking genes across annual and perennial plant species by applying computational pipelines and network frameworks to build context specific gene expression models. The study will integrate public sequencing and live cell imaging repositories by standardizing metadata, processing raw RNA sequencing data into comparable expression matrices, and connecting distinct species datasets through genome anchored orthology maps. This research will identify novel regulatory genes that connect endomembrane trafficking with thermal physiology to inform future agricultural strategies for mitigating heat induced yield loss in essential crops.
abstract_original: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. title: From Nucleosome Mechanics to Cell-Type Identity: A Multiscale Synthesis of Chromatin Polymer Physics, Condensate Biochemistry, and Single-Cell 3D Genomes to Explain Disease-Relevant Genome Folding in the Human Brain
title_norm: from nucleosome mechanics to celltype identity a multiscale synthesis of chromatin polymer physics condensate biochemistry and singlecell 3d genomes to explain diseaserelevant genome folding in the human brain
abstract_text: Mesoscale chromatin organization links nanometer nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensates to megabase compartments across brain cell types, representing a critical mechanism underlying cell type specific diseases including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Current high resolution structural and population datasets remain disconnected, leaving a gap in mechanistic models that connect nucleosome biophysics to cell type specific chromatin folding and genetic disease risks. This project will build a multiscale chromatin simulation framework by parameterizing coarse grained polymer models with structural data, executing mesoscale simulations to test condensate forming mechanisms, and mapping genetic variants using statistical colocalization analyses. The research will integrate cryo EM structures and single cell diploid 3D genomes to parameterize polymer interactions, subsequently overlaying the predicted physical chromatin states onto brain wide eQTL atlases and GWAS summary statistics. This framework will provide a mechanistic explanation for why specific variants cause cell type restricted phenotypes, converting correlative genetic associations in psychiatric and neuroimmune conditions into testable structural hypotheses.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale chromatin organization requires models linking the biophysics of nucleosomes to large scale folding in brains. Current studies detail structural physics and genomic architectures but these distinct fields remain disconnected from datasets of population genetics. This study builds a simulation framework to provide structural explanations for how specific genetic variants cause restricted human diseases. The core strategy parameterizes models of polymers and benchmarks simulated structures against single cell genomes before overlaying physical states. Key methods include simulations of mesoscale chromatin and comparisons of nested models alongside approaches for stratified enrichment and colocalization. Results undergo validation against empirical single cell structures and orthogonal datasets using specific protocols that are registered in advance. Datasets feature single cell genomes and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures from public repositories like the Sequence Read Archive. The team will harmonize structural measurements to parameterize interaction terms before overlaying predicted annotations onto datasets of population genetics. The team addresses incompatible resolutions and formats through structural integration sessions and the collaborative development of bridging computational pipelines. The timeline involves two workshops per year and virtual sprints to achieve three phases of parameterization and genomic mapping. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because no single laboratory possesses the required expertise across structural biophysics and genomics. The team will deposit harmonized data into public repositories and publish software featuring containerized environments under open source licenses. The team spans multiple career stages and offers trainees funded workshops alongside educational modules that pair biophysics with genomics.

abstract_original: A central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how nanometer-scale nucleosome-nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensate formation give rise to megabase-scale chromatin compartments and loop domains that differ systematically across human cell types—and how these emergent architectures channel genetic risk into cell-type-specific disease phenotypes. This gap sits squarely at the mesoscale NCEMS prioritizes: it cannot be resolved by structural biology, polymer physics, or population genetics alone, but requires their synthesis. This Working Group proposes to integrate four classes of existing public data that have never been jointly modeled: (1) single-cell diploid 3D genome structures (Dip-C/scHi-C) spanning dozens of human and mouse brain cell types; (2) nucleosome- and chromatin-fiber-resolution structural and simulation data (cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, mesoscale oligonucleosome models, cohesin-loop Hi-C perturbation datasets); (3) biochemical and structural characterizations of chromatin-associated condensate components (corepressor oligomers, histone-modifying enzyme complexes, RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation); and (4) population-scale functional genomics linking genetic variation to cell-type-specific gene expression and disease risk (brain-wide eQTL atlases, GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease). Our central hypothesis is that cell-type-specific genome folding emerges from a hierarchy of physical rules—entropic and electrostatic steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators at the nucleosome scale, cooperative condensate formation by transcriptional corepressor/coactivator complexes at the sub-domain scale, and loop-extrusion/compartmentalization dynamics at the topologically associating domain scale—and that this hierarchy is a mechanistic intermediate between GWAS variants and their cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. We will build coarse-grained, mechanistically grounded polymer models of chromatin fibers parameterized from structural and biophysical data, validate emergent compartment and loop predictions against single-cell Dip-C structures across neuronal and glial subtypes, and test whether condensate-forming regulatory complexes (e.g., corepressor tetramers, methyltransferase-associated assemblies, RNA-binding phase-separating proteins) quantitatively explain observed heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences between cell types. We will then map disease-associated eQTL and GWAS loci onto these physically resolved chromatin states to ask whether variants disrupting predicted condensate-nucleation or loop-anchor regions preferentially explain the cell-type specificity of psychiatric versus neuroimmune disease associations already reported in public datasets. This effort requires collaboration across structural biophysics, polymer theory, single-cell genomics, and population-scale systems immunology/genetics—expertise that no single lab possesses, but that our team collectively spans. Deliverables include an open, versioned multiscale chromatin simulation framework linked to public single-cell 3D genome and eQTL/GWAS resources, reproducible pipelines for condensate-informed loop-domain prediction, and training modules pairing biophysical modeling with population genomics for graduate students and postdocs across participating institutions. By unifying nucleosome-scale biophysics with population-scale genetics through existing data alone, this project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: resolving how physical emergence at the mesoscale of chromatin organization constrains and explains cellular identity and disease susceptibility in the human brain.

title: Functional Redundancy as a Mesoscale Buffer: Synthesizing Ancient and Modern Metagenomes with Host Proteo-Genomic Atlases to Test the Stability of Microbiome-Host Molecular Modules
title_norm: functional redundancy as a mesoscale buffer synthesizing ancient and modern metagenomes with host proteogenomic atlases to test the stability of microbiomehost molecular modules
abstract_text: Microbial ecology investigates how microbial functional modules couple to host molecular physiology, a critical phenomenon because microbiome associated host phenotypes remain highly stable despite extensive variation in underlying microbial taxonomy. To determine if functional modules associate with host circulating proteins and metabolites independently of taxa over evolutionary time, this data synthesis project will apply DIAMOND, MEGAN, and Mendelian randomization to diverse metagenomes. Data from the Human Microbiome Project, UK Biobank, and ancient metagenome archives will be standardized into a cross cohort functional module abundance atlas and linked to host proteogenomic profiles using statistical genetics methods. This research will provide a novel framework to differentiate between emergent functional properties and taxon specific correlations, significantly improving the prioritization of biomarkers and therapeutic targets for microbiome related conditions.
full_text: This microbial ecology project studies microbial functional modules to address gaps in testing across modern and evolutionary timescales. Host phenotypes associated with microbiomes remain stable but understanding of this functional stability across different eras is incomplete. The primary research question explores if these functional associations remain conserved over time to prioritize biomarkers for therapeutics. The overall study design utilizes a data synthesis approach to construct indices of redundancy and integrate host data. Key methods include algorithms for taxonomic binning and models of statistical genetics such as Mendelian randomization and colocalization. The proposed study will validate results by testing findings against independent modern cohorts and datasets of ancient genomes. The project utilizes datasets from the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) and the GWAS Catalog alongside archives of ancient metagenomes. The team will integrate distinct datasets by standardizing information into an atlas of abundances for linkage with genetics. Known limitations of DNA damage and exogenous contamination will be mitigated using established protocols for authentication and screening. Proposed milestones consist of four consecutive stages including the harmonization of metagenomes and integration of host genetic data. The project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to synthesize specialized fields like theory of phylogenetic networks and statistical genetics. The team will release datasets under open licenses and containerize analytical code for public availability on platforms like GitHub. The team includes two postdoctoral researchers and one graduate student receiving cross disciplinary training in analysis of ancient DNA.

abstract_original:
A central puzzle in microbial ecology is why host phenotypes associated with the microbiome often remain stable despite enormous taxonomic turnover in microbial communities across individuals, populations, and evolutionary time. One resolution is that functional modules—conserved sets of microbial genes encoding metabolic pathways such as short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—represent an emergent, mesoscale level of biological organization that buffers taxonomic variability and directly couples to host molecular physiology. This project will synthesize publicly available shotgun metagenomic data spanning contemporary human cohorts (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and ancient microbiomes (dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived shotgun datasets from Paleolithic through historical periods) with large-scale human proteogenomic and metabolomic resources (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, plasma cis-pQTL maps, NMR metabolomic panels) to test whether specific microbial functional modules show consistent, genetically anchored associations with host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of which taxa or strains carry them, and whether this coupling is stable across evolutionary timescales.

We will reprocess all metagenomes using a standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based taxonomic and functional binning pipeline to build a harmonized cross-cohort, cross-era atlas of functional module abundance, explicitly accounting for degradation and contamination artifacts characteristic of low-biomass ancient samples using established authentication and decontamination frameworks. Strain- and gene-family-level phylogenetic network methods (NeighborNet and related split-decomposition approaches) will be used to quantify the degree of taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module, generating a quantitative 'redundancy index' per pathway. In parallel, we will mine existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics and cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL resources to identify host genetic variants associated with both circulating protein/metabolite levels and microbiome functional module abundance, applying Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization to test causal or bidirectional relationships between microbial functional capacity and host proteomic/metabolomic states. Modules showing robust host-molecular coupling in modern cohorts will then be evaluated in ancient samples paired with available ancient human genomic data, providing a natural, deep-time test of whether these host-microbiome molecular relationships are evolutionarily conserved or population/era-specific artifacts of recent lifestyle change.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise unavailable within any single laboratory: metagenomic algorithm development and phylogenetic network theory, ancient DNA authentication and low-biomass contamination control, and human proteogenomic/statistical genetics analysis at biobank scale. The resulting open-access resource—a versioned, reproducible workflow and 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' spanning contemporary and ancient timescales—will provide the field with a principled, falsifiable framework for identifying which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust emergent mesoscale properties versus incidental, taxon-specific correlations, directly informing biomarker and therapeutic target prioritization in microbiome-related disease research. All code, intermediate outputs, and harmonized datasets will be deposited under FAIR principles, with structured training modules for graduate students and postdocs spanning computational metagenomics, paleogenomics, and human genetics.

title: Mapping the Coupling Between Regulatory Cell-State Transitions and Mesoscale Condensate Architecture Across the Bacterial Kingdom
title_norm: mapping the coupling between regulatory cellstate transitions and mesoscale condensate architecture across the bacterial kingdom
abstract_text: The research domain of bacterial cell biology and biomolecular condensate biophysics examines phase separated mesoscale protein assemblies, which are important because bacteria utilize these structures for cellular compartmentalization. The critical scientific gap is whether gene regulatory networks systematically encode the spatial reorganization and phase assembly of bacterial mesoscale structures during physiological transitions. The primary objective will create a cross species atlas linking bacterial regulatory states to phase separation propensity by applying sequence based biophysical predictors, associative polymer models, and mixed effects regression to synthesize transcriptomic and proteomic data. This project will integrate PRECISE, COLOMBOS, PaxDb, ALEdb, and isolate repositories by harmonizing metadata with controlled vocabulary ontologies and mapping matched transcriptomic and proteomic data to genome wide phase separation propensity scores. The resulting cross species atlas will establish whether bacterial spatial organization represents an actively programmed regulatory output rather than a passive biophysical byproduct.
full_text: This project merges bacterial biology and condensate biophysics to determine if regulatory networks encode phase separated assemblies during transitions. The team will build a cross species atlas to determine if spatial organization represents an actively programmed regulatory output. A three phase computational strategy will integrate transcriptomic and proteomic data with polymer physics models of condensate phase behavior. The researchers will apply sequence based biophysical predictors (catGRANULE) alongside associative polymer models and mixed effects regression techniques. Transcript level inferences will be cross validated against protein abundance data and model predictions will undergo benchmarking against experimental literature. The study will utilize established RNA-seq collections (PRECISE) and the PaxDb proteomic database alongside the ALEdb evolution dataset. The team will integrate datasets by harmonizing metadata with controlled vocabulary ontologies and mapping information to phase separation scores. The researchers will mitigate technical batch effects and phylogenetic dependencies by controlling for these variables within mixed effects models. Milestones include completing an expression to propensity atlas and conducting biophysical translation alongside the execution of evolutionary genomic integration. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because simultaneous expertise across network biology and condensate biophysics exceeds single laboratory capabilities. The team will share data and code via public repositories (Zenodo) while openly distributing all scientific findings through preprints. The research group includes principal investigators and trainees who will receive cross disciplinary training across evolutionary biology and biophysics.

Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles, yet an increasing number of proteinaceous mesoscale assemblies—BR-bodies, PopZ microdomains, ParB/parS partition complexes, cold-shock and stress granules—are now recognized as functionally important, phase-separated or phase-separation-like structures. What remains unknown is whether the assembly and disassembly of these structures is systematically encoded in the transcriptional and regulatory logic of the cell, such that physiological transitions (growth phase, stress, quorum-sensing state, biofilm commitment) predictably reorganize the mesoscale proteome. This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

The working group will first build a cross-species atlas linking condition-specific transcriptional/proteomic states to the predicted phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome, testing whether physiological transitions (e.g., entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress) are consistently accompanied by co-regulated shifts in the abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich proteins relative to their low-propensity partners. This addresses a mesoscale question central to NCEMS's mission: does gene-regulatory network architecture function, in part, as a control layer for mesoscale self-organization, translating discrete transcriptional states into emergent, spatially organized biomolecular assemblies? Second, using biophysical/polymer-based condensate models—of the associative-polymer type used to explain multiphase architecture and viscosity tuning in reconstituted systems—the team will translate measured or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into predictions of condensate composition, phase boundaries, and internal architecture, generating testable hypotheses about which regulons are poised to nucleate or dissolve specific mesoscale structures under specific conditions. Third, the team will exploit existing evolution-experiment and clinical-isolate genomic datasets to ask whether naturally occurring or experimentally evolved loss-of-function mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pumps, two-component systems) shift the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins, thereby altering emergent mesoscale organization as a byproduct of adaptive evolution—paralleling known cases where regulatory mutations have unexpected downstream physiological consequences.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and regulatory network biology with quantitative condensate biophysics and polymer theory, a combination not resident in any single laboratory. It leverages exclusively existing public datasets, produces an open, versioned, and queryable atlas linking transcriptomic state to predicted mesoscale organization across bacterial diversity, and provides trainees hands-on experience integrating heterogeneous omics, evolutionary, and biophysical modeling data—directly building the data-science workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously unaddressed question about the origins of mesoscale order in cells lacking organelles.

title: Nonlinear Collapse of Protein Interaction Networks at Stability Thresholds: A Cross-Kingdom Synthesis of Deep Mutational Scanning and Interactome Data
title_norm: nonlinear collapse of protein interaction networks at stability thresholds a crosskingdom synthesis of deep mutational scanning and interactome data
abstract_text: Molecular systems biology explores how interaction networks buffer destabilizing mutations, a phenomenon crucial for understanding proteome scale robustness in human membrane proteins and plant cytosolic immune regulators. This project will determine whether network connectivity dictates mutation tolerance by harmonizing stability and topology data to model nonlinear functional collapse thresholds using changepoint detection, percolation simulations, and single cell transcriptomic coexpression via a modular Python pipeline. Stability measurements from MaveDB and ProteinGym, interactomes from BioGRID and STRING, and evolutionary data from gnomAD will be synthesized by standardizing variant coordinates and linking them to unified graph representations. This research will yield a quantitative framework predicting when mutations become pathogenic or adaptive, informing variant effect interpretation in human diseases and clarifying plant immune network robustness.
full_text: This molecular systems biology project investigates if interaction network positions predict phenotypic tolerance to biophysically destabilizing protein mutations. Large independent datasets demonstrate nonlinear mutational effects but lack integration to explain phenotypic robustness across proteome scale networks. The study asks if network connectivity dictates mutation tolerance thresholds to establish predictive frameworks for disease and adaptation. The design harmonizes datasets to model interactions of thermodynamic stability and network topology using single cell transcriptomic profiles. A modular Python pipeline will execute network centrality calculations and changepoint detection and percolation simulations for robustness analysis. The simulated network collapse points will undergo validation against independent phenotypic measurements of surface trafficking and immune signaling. Data sources incorporate thermodynamic measurements from MaveDB and interaction networks from BioGRID alongside public single cell transcriptomic atlases. Synthesis involves standardizing thermodynamic units and mapping evolutionary annotations to unified graph representations of interactomes with centrality metrics. The team will mitigate heterogeneous data structures and curation biases through rigorous data harmonization and statistical sensitivity analyses. Proposed milestones sequentially encompass initial data harmonization and computational modeling before the integration of single cell transcriptomic datasets. The massive analytical scale necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration combining distinct expertise in protein thermodynamics and network systems biology. The researchers will share harmonized datasets and open source code through public repositories to ensure transparent open access. Graduate students and one postdoctoral researcher from three institutions will receive cross disciplinary training in biophysical network modeling.
