Skeletal muscle exhibits striking emergent behavior: molecular changes in signaling, chromatin state, ribosome production, autophagy, immune activity, and mechanical response collectively produce higher-order outcomes such as hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, or functional decline. Yet a central unresolved question remains: why do similar anabolic or mechanical cues produce robust growth in some contexts but maladaptive inflammation, impaired repair, or wasting in others? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define and model an emergent property we call “translational reserve”: the coordinated capacity of muscle cells and their local niche to expand ribosome biogenesis, maintain protein synthesis, buffer proteostatic stress, and support tissue remodeling under mechanical or inflammatory challenge.

This project will use only publicly available datasets to integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-scale information across human and animal skeletal muscle studies. Data sources will include bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq from exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, muscular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and injury models; public proteomics and phosphoproteomics datasets related to mTOR signaling, ribosome assembly, autophagy, and inflammatory pathways; DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility datasets where available; ribosome profiling and translation-associated datasets from muscle and related cell types; and histological or imaging-derived public metadata on fiber size, fiber type, fibrosis, immune infiltration, and functional outcomes. The project will harmonize these heterogeneous resources into a shared cross-species atlas of muscle adaptation states.

The central hypothesis is that tissue-level muscle outcomes emerge from nonlinear interactions among three mesoscale modules: nucleolar/ribosome biogenesis capacity, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche signaling. We will test this by developing an AI-driven multiscale integration framework combining graph neural networks, interpretable latent variable models, and mathematical dynamical modeling. The graph representation will connect genes, proteins, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, disease contexts, and phenotypic outcomes. GPU-accelerated workflows will enable large-scale reanalysis of sequencing and methylation datasets, standardized feature extraction, and scalable model training across many public studies. Mathematical models will then translate learned network structure into dynamic hypotheses about threshold behavior, feedback loops, and tipping points that separate adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling.

The expected product is not merely a catalog of exercise-responsive genes, but a predictive synthesis of how molecular and cellular modules combine to generate emergent muscle phenotypes. We will identify conserved and context-specific signatures of translational reserve, determine whether inflammatory disease shifts muscle toward a low-reserve state, and evaluate whether ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, and immune-cell composition jointly predict fiber growth or fibrosis better than any single pathway. Cross-species analyses will distinguish mechanisms conserved between rodent overload models and human training or disease cohorts, while cell-type-resolved analyses will reveal how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune cells contribute to the emergent tissue response.

NCEMS support is essential because this effort requires coordinated expertise in muscle biology, translational control, inflammation, high-performance computing, graph-based AI, and mechanistic mathematical modeling, as well as community agreement on data standards and reproducible workflows. The working group will release an open atlas, curated metadata schema, analysis pipelines, trained models, and interactive visualization tools. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive cross-training in muscle physiology, public-data reuse, GPU-enabled bioinformatics, network modeling, and open collaborative science. By synthesizing dispersed public data into a mechanistic, predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how molecular-scale control of protein production and stress buffering gives rise to cell- and tissue-scale muscle adaptation or failure.

title_norm: a public data atlas linking disorderedregion sequence grammar to emergent condensate material states
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates, which form through multivalent interactions involving intrinsically disordered regions and nucleic acids, encompass the material state transitions of RNA binding protein granules, transcriptional and chromatin condensates, and stress responsive condensates. Currently, public data remain dispersed across isolated biological subfields, leaving no framework to link the molecular sequence features of disordered regions to the resulting mesoscale material properties of condensates. This project will determine which combinations of molecular features dictate condensate material states by synthesizing public data through text mining and manual curation to train machine learning models such as gradient boosted trees. Information from diverse databases including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DisProt, UniProt, and AlphaFold will be integrated by mapping heterogeneous experimental observations onto a multidimensional condensate material ontology utilizing automated retrieval pipelines. The resulting atlas will map these relationships to distinguish the physical rules governing typical cellular organization from those driving pathological protein aggregation in diseases such as neurodegeneration.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates emerge from many weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level answer to a central question: which molecular features determine whether a condensate remains a dynamic cellular compartment, becomes a gel-like regulatory hub, or crosses into aberrant aggregation? We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate public sequence, biophysical, imaging, proteomic, and disease-variant data to build a predictive atlas connecting disordered-region molecular grammar to mesoscale condensate material properties.

The working group will assemble and harmonize existing public data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, and published supplementary datasets reporting phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, viscosity proxies, SAXS/NMR-derived ensemble parameters, turbidity, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. The project will focus on three biologically important condensate classes that are rarely analyzed together: RNA-binding protein granules linked to neurodegeneration, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates involving polyamines, phosphorylation, oxidation, or other cellular-state variables.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate material state is not encoded by single features such as net charge or aromatic content alone, but by higher-order patterns: sticker valence and spacing, charge blockiness, transient structure propensity, partner valence, nucleic acid context, post-translational modification state, and cellular concentration regimes. These features jointly produce emergent mesoscale properties that can be inferred only by integrating heterogeneous datasets across proteins, organisms, experimental modalities, and disease contexts.

The synthesis will proceed in four coordinated activities. First, we will create an open condensate-material ontology that standardizes experimental descriptors such as liquid-like exchange, viscoelasticity, aging, demixing, gelation, and irreversible aggregation. Second, we will extract quantitative and semi-quantitative material-state labels from public tables, figures, repositories, and curated literature using reproducible text-mining and human-in-the-loop annotation. Third, we will compute interpretable polymer-physics and sequence-patterning features for disordered regions and combine them with PTM, mutation, abundance, localization, RNA-binding, and interaction-network features. Fourth, we will train benchmarked machine-learning and statistical models to predict condensate state transitions and identify conserved physical rules shared across neurodegenerative proteins, transcription factors, histone tails, and synthetic condensate scaffolds.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, normalize, and interpret the dispersed data spanning biophysics, cell biology, neurodegeneration, genomics, image analysis, and polymer theory. The working group will bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin organization, neurodegenerative disease, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly licensed database, FAIR workflows, benchmark datasets, interactive visualization tools, and training modules for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible data synthesis. By transforming scattered public observations into an integrated mesoscale atlas, the project will provide a general framework for predicting how molecular disorder gives rise to emergent cellular organization and when that organization becomes pathological.

title: A Comparative Multi-Omics Atlas of Reversible Metabolic Suppression Across Mammalian Hibernators
title_norm: a comparative multiomics atlas of reversible metabolic suppression across mammalian hibernators
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation requires conserved and lineage specific molecular programs for reversible metabolic suppression and tissue preservation, and detecting shared biological principles among these processes remains critical for evolutionary and physiological research. Current multi omics knowledge remains fragmented by species and tissue, lacking a unified comparative framework to identify how these molecular programs combine across biological scales. This project will build an integrated comparative multi omics atlas to determine how diverse mammals reversibly reorganize cellular energy use without pathological damage, and will apply machine learning alongside evolutionary models to identify tissue specific hibernation modules. The analysis will integrate public bulk and single cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from primary repositories using standardized processing workflows, orthology mapping, and random effects meta analysis. The resulting comparative atlas will evaluate cross scale synthesis, separating true hibernation mechanisms from generic stress responses to reveal whether metabolic suppression relies on conserved pathways or convergent regulatory architecture.

Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. This working group will synthesize existing public data to ask a central question: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs allow diverse mammals to reversibly reorganize cellular energy use during hibernation without pathological damage? We will build an open, comparative atlas integrating publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq where available, proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals. The project will focus on emergent mesoscale processes that link molecules to cellular and tissue phenotypes, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-cell state shifts. By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. For example, we will evaluate whether mitochondrial genes, lipid-handling genes, circadian regulators, and inflammatory mediators form conserved cross-tissue network motifs that predict hibernation state better than any single tissue or pathway. We will also compare natural hibernation datasets with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, and aging models to distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic stress responses. The resulting resource will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic depression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular changes across tissues. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires a transdisciplinary working group spanning evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, data harmonization, and phylogenetic statistics. No single laboratory currently has the breadth of expertise or the capacity to curate, standardize, and jointly analyze these diverse public datasets at community scale. Deliverables will include a FAIR hibernation multi-omics atlas, reproducible analysis workflows, orthology-aware gene module annotations, interactive network visualizations, and training materials for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. By synthesizing existing public data across mammals, this project will reveal how molecular programs combine into emergent cellular and physiological states, while creating a reusable open-science platform for future studies of metabolic resilience.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent biomolecular condensate behavior can be predicted from evolutionarily conserved networks of residue, domain, and motif couplings within multivalent proteins and their interaction partners. The guiding hypothesis is that many condensate-forming systems are regulated by hidden coupling architectures: perturbations at folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, RNA-binding surfaces, post-translational modification sites, or ion-binding regions propagate through molecular ensembles to alter mesoscale assembly thresholds and material states.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate protein family alignments from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and model-organism databases; structural models and experimental structures from AlphaFold DB, PDB, SASBDB, and integrative structure repositories; condensate annotations and phase behavior measurements from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and curated literature-derived datasets; public mutational scans and variant-effect datasets from MaveDB, ClinVar, cBioPortal, and organismal resources; proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets from PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange; RNA-binding and chromatin-associated interaction datasets from ENCODE and related repositories; and reusable molecular simulation trajectories from public simulation archives where available. These heterogeneous resources will be harmonized into a FAIR, versioned knowledge graph linking sequence features, coevolutionary constraints, structural contacts, dynamic ensembles, modification sites, disease or engineered variants, and observed condensate phenotypes.

A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how evolutionary changes in genes and metabolic reactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular properties such as membrane composition, lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisome activity, and stress-dependent organelle organization. These properties are not encoded by single genes; they emerge from coordinated flux through lipid, amino acid, redox, and energy metabolism. Yet the public data needed to connect evolutionary pressures, metabolic network architecture, and mesoscale cellular organization now exist across human populations, model organisms, microbes, plants, and immune cell systems. This working group will synthesize these resources to ask: which metabolic network modules are repeatedly targeted by evolution and environmental response because they control emergent mesoscale organization?

The project will integrate only publicly available data: population genomic datasets from humans and other species; comparative genomes and orthology resources; transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets from environmental perturbations including temperature, diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, and immune activation; genome-scale metabolic reconstructions from BiGG, ModelSEED, Human-GEM, plant metabolic databases, and organism-specific reconstructions; and public microscopy-derived organelle and cellular morphology datasets from resources such as the Image Data Resource and Cell Painting repositories. We will construct a cross-species reaction-centered knowledge graph linking genes, orthologs, variants, selection statistics, reactions, metabolites, lipid classes, predicted flux states, and mesoscale phenotypes. This graph will allow evolutionary signals and cellular systems measurements to be analyzed in a shared metabolic coordinate system rather than as disconnected gene lists.

Methodologically, the group will combine interpretable population-genetic machine learning with constraint-based metabolic modeling. Deep learning models trained on simulated neutral and selected haplotypes will identify genomic regions whose evolutionary histories are inconsistent with neutrality, while interpretable feature attribution will distinguish selection acting on individual loci from selection on coordinated metabolic modules. In parallel, context-specific genome-scale metabolic models will be reconstructed from public multi-omic datasets to infer flux reorganization under environmental and cellular states. A synthesis layer will then test whether selected genes are enriched not merely in pathways, but in flux-controlling modules predicted to alter mesoscale properties such as phospholipid saturation, sterol balance, acyl-chain remodeling, mitochondrial redox coupling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, and lipid storage capacity.

The expected outcome is a generalizable atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules that generate mesoscale cellular organization across species and conditions. The project will address whether convergent environmental pressures produce convergent metabolic network solutions, whether human adaptive loci disproportionately affect emergent membrane and organelle states, and whether stress-responsive flux modules in cells correspond to modules recurrently shaped by natural selection across populations and taxa. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it spans population genetics, genome-scale metabolic modeling, lipid metabolism, comparative genomics, machine learning interpretability, and image-based cell phenotyping—expertise and data integration beyond the scope of a single laboratory.

All workflows, harmonized datasets, metabolic model annotations, trained models, and interactive visualizations will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary hackathons and reproducible analysis teams, gaining experience in evolutionary genomics, metabolic network modeling, public data integration, and interpretable AI for molecular and cellular emergence.

title: Proteome Flux Codes for Emergent Mesoscale Remodeling During Cellular Stress and Disease
title_norm: proteome flux codes for emergent mesoscale remodeling during cellular stress and disease
abstract_text: Cellular biology research investigates the reorganization of mesoscale protein systems and proteome flux during stress and cardiometabolic diseases, a crucial area because static abundance measurements fail to capture rate dependent mesoscale reorganization. It remains unclear how dynamic molecular flux processes combine to produce emergent mesoscale cellular structures and phenotypes because measurements remain fragmented across disparate repositories, technologies, and analytical conventions. This project will define generalizable proteome flux codes by integrating public multi omics datasets into an interoperable atlas, utilizing unsupervised clustering, supervised machine learning, and hierarchical Bayesian models to link molecular flux signatures to cellular outcomes. The analysis will integrate ribosome profiling, RNA sequencing, and single cell transcriptomics datasets from repositories including GEO, PRIDE, and CPTAC, harmonizing turnover and translation measurements via mixed effect models accounting for metadata. This research will produce predictive dynamic models of proteome flux, providing a vital framework to differentiate between reversible adaptive cellular remodeling and persistent pathological restructuring.
full_text: This project in cellular biology investigates how processes of molecular flux produce emergent protein structures during stress and disease. The researchers will deposit data in open repositories and maintain version controlled code alongside executable notebooks and tutorials for the community. Cells often respond to stress not by changing the abundance of individual molecules alone, but by reorganizing mesoscale protein systems: ribonucleoprotein assemblies, cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds, extracellular matrices, metabolic enzyme clusters, and organelle-associated protein communities. A central unsolved question is how molecular flux through the proteome—translation, degradation, post-translational modification, disorder-mediated interaction, and localization—combines to produce these emergent cellular structures and phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define generalizable “proteome flux codes” that predict when changes in protein synthesis and turnover produce mesoscale remodeling across stress, aging, and cardiometabolic disease contexts.

This working group will integrate only publicly available datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Core inputs will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-labeling and protein turnover datasets, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, protein disorder and structural annotations, subcellular localization resources, protein interaction networks, phase-separation and condensate-associated protein catalogs, and public single-cell or bulk transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from stress models, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, cardiovascular tissues, cancer stress states, and aging-related systems. Rather than treating mRNA, translation, protein abundance, and degradation as separate regulatory layers, we will build harmonized models of protein residence time, production rate, degradation rate, modification state, and mesoscale membership.

The central hypothesis is that emergent mesoscale remodeling is governed by coordinated shifts in proteome flux, especially among proteins with long residence times, intrinsically disordered regions, modification-rich segments, scaffold-like interaction properties, or compartment-specific localization. These features may explain why some cellular responses are rapid and reversible, whereas others become persistent, pathological, or tissue-specific. We will test this through three synthesis aims. First, we will create an interoperable atlas of proteome flux across public datasets, with uncertainty-aware normalization of turnover, translation, and abundance measurements across organisms, cell types, perturbations, and technologies. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with mesoscale assemblies, including stress granule-like systems, nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated networks, mitochondrial and metabolic complexes, extracellular matrix remodeling modules, and cytoskeletal or contractile structures. Third, we will develop predictive machine-learning and mechanistic network models that link molecular flux signatures to higher-order cellular outcomes such as stress adaptation, proteostasis collapse, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, and age-associated remodeling.

This project requires NCEMS-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate, reconcile, and model the diverse public datasets needed to connect translation dynamics, proteome turnover, structural disorder, post-translational regulation, and disease-relevant cell phenotypes. The working group would bring together experts in proteomics, ribosome profiling, cardiovascular and stem-cell models, structural bioinformatics, stress biology, network science, and open computational infrastructure. Deliverables will include a FAIR public proteome-flux atlas, reproducible workflows, benchmark datasets for turnover inference, interactive visualization tools, and trainee-led tutorials on integrative molecular data synthesis. By focusing on how molecular rates and regulatory layers combine to generate mesoscale biological organization, this project directly addresses NCEMS priorities and offers a new framework for understanding emergent cellular behavior from existing public data.

title: Inferring Conserved Mesoscale Kinetic Programs from Public Spatial Omics and Fluorescence Microscopy Atlases
title_norm: inferring conserved mesoscale kinetic programs from public spatial omics and fluorescence microscopy atlases
abstract_text: While molecular and cellular biology defines cell states primarily by transcript abundance, mesoscale kinetic organization encompassing RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, and molecular mobility represents a crucial phenomenon for understanding complex biological transitions. The lack of integration between single cell gene expression profiles and subcellular imaging data currently limits the understanding of how emergent mesoscale cellular behaviors function independently of transcript abundance. This project will determine whether diverse cellular transitions follow conserved mesoscale kinetic programs by extracting biophysical features from harmonized public datasets and applying a hierarchical Bayesian multimodal latent state model to identify recurring programs. Single cell transcriptomics, proteomic resources, and fluorescence microscopy datasets will be integrated by mapping heterogeneous measurements into a shared latent representation through probabilistic alignment utilizing cell type, marker genes, and spatial context parameters. This research will establish a spatially grounded biophysical model that shifts cell state definitions, explaining how different biological systems generate similar cellular phenotypes using differing marker genes.
full_text: The field of cellular biology lacks integration of single cell profiles and subcellular images to elucidate mesoscale kinetic organization. This project investigates whether diverse cellular transitions share conserved mesoscale programs to shift toward a spatially grounded biophysical model. This data synthesis study harmonizes public datasets and extracts biophysical features to identify recurring programs across three biological systems. The analytical approach relies on a hierarchical Bayesian multimodal model alongside probabilistic feature extraction and alignment of cell states. The team will validate results using held out datasets and baseline comparisons alongside negative controls with randomized coordinates. Cell states are usually defined by transcriptional profiles, yet many consequential state transitions emerge from mesoscale organization: RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane localization, molecular mobility, and organelle-associated trafficking. A macrophage-exposed tumor cell, a differentiating neural progenitor, or a stressed neuron may share little transcriptomic identity, but may converge on similar mesoscale kinetic solutions such as altered nuclear export, enhanced membrane-proximal signaling, or increased residence time of regulatory proteins in subcellular compartments. This working group will test the hypothesis that diverse cellular transitions are governed by a small set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred by synthesizing existing public spatial omics, proteomics, and fluorescence microscopy data.

We will build an open synthesis framework that links three public data classes that are rarely analyzed together. First, we will harmonize single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets from public repositories, including brain development and adult brain atlases, tumor microenvironment datasets, MERFISH/seqFISH-style measurements with subcellular RNA localization, and spatial cancer atlases. Second, we will integrate proteomic and immunofluorescence resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, public CODEX/IMC datasets, and subcellular protein localization maps. Third, we will mine public microscopy repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive for live-cell, single-particle, FRAP/FCS, super-resolution, and organelle-tracking datasets that report protein mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, or trafficking dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated.

The central methodological innovation will be a Bayesian multimodal model that translates heterogeneous public measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Rather than treating images as qualitative annotations, the framework will extract probabilistic features including nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning, local transcript density, protein puncta size and number, apparent oligomeric state, organelle adjacency, membrane enrichment, and effective mobility or residence-time estimates where time-resolved data exist. These features will be linked to matched or harmonized transcriptomic cell states using batch-aware integration and uncertainty propagation. The model will explicitly account for differences in optical resolution, fluorophore sampling, segmentation quality, and assay modality, enabling principled comparison across datasets and laboratories.

We will apply the framework to three biological transitions with abundant public data and strong mesoscale relevance: neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling of tumor cells and immune neighborhoods, and cellular stress states involving mitochondrial and membrane-trafficking pathways. Across these systems, we will ask whether transcriptionally distinct cell types reuse common mesoscale programs; whether spatially localized RNAs predict protein compartmentalization or mobility; and whether emergent cellular phenotypes are better explained by inferred kinetic features than by gene expression alone. Expected products include an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs, reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public microscopy data, benchmark datasets for spatial omics–image integration, and candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in single-cell and spatial data integration, statistical optics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule biophysics, image analysis, cell-state biology, and open data engineering. The working group will include trainees as core contributors through hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules on spatial omics, microscopy uncertainty, and probabilistic modeling. All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.

This working group will test the hypothesis that tRNA modifications act as mesoscale control points by reshaping ribosome traffic, protein complex stoichiometry, and chromatin-regulatory assemblies, thereby generating emergent epigenomic and immune phenotypes across microbes and human cells. The project will use only publicly available data and will synthesize information across RNA modification biology, ribosome profiling, proteomics, structural modeling, single-cell genomics, and microbial metabolism.

We will build an open, cross-kingdom atlas linking tRNA modification capacity to translation and cellular phenotype. Public resources will include MODOMICS and curated bacterial and eukaryotic tRNA modification enzyme annotations; published tRNA modification mapping datasets; ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, and proteomics from bacteria, yeast, mammalian cells, cancer models, immune perturbation studies, neurodegeneration cohorts, and metabolic stress datasets; public single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq atlases from tumor, brain, and cardiovascular tissues; microbial genome and metagenome datasets with annotated micronutrient and RNA-modification pathways; and public protein structures from PDB and AlphaFold. No new experimental data will be generated.

The scientific question is deliberately multiscale: when a tRNA modification is lost, altered, or metabolite-limited, which codon contexts experience altered elongation, which proteins become selectively under- or over-produced, and which higher-order cellular structures or regulatory programs are most vulnerable? We will develop a codon-aware synthesis framework that integrates ribosome pausing signatures with transcript abundance, protein abundance, protein complex membership, post-translational modification data, and chromatin accessibility. Graph-based imputation and feature-propagation methods will harmonize sparse single-cell and bulk datasets, while interpretable machine-learning models will identify conserved translation-sensitive modules. Structural and coarse-grained molecular modeling will be used not to create new simulations as primary data, but to contextualize public structures of affected chromatin regulators, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, and immune signaling proteins in terms of complex formation, DNA engagement, and mesoscale assembly potential.

The expected outcome is a quantitative map of how nucleotide-scale chemical information propagates to emergent mesoscale organization. We will focus on three synthesis products: first, a conserved catalog of codon- and modification-sensitive translation bottlenecks across organisms; second, a ranked set of chromatin, immune, and metabolic protein complexes whose stoichiometry is predicted to be unusually sensitive to tRNA modification state; and third, a set of cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient availability, host tRNA modification capacity, ribosome pausing, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. This framework could help explain why similar transcriptional programs diverge into distinct proteomic or epigenomic outcomes, and why microbial metabolites or transporter variation can have unexpectedly broad cellular effects.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in microbial genomics, RNA modification biology, single-cell data integration, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural modeling, and AI. The working group will release harmonized datasets, reproducible workflows, interactive network browsers, and training modules for trainees in open, data-intensive molecular synthesis research.

Public RNA-seq and proteomics datasets from pathogens, environmental bacteria, cyanobacteria, anaerobes, and host-associated communities will be reanalyzed to determine when candidate compartment loci are co-regulated with iron limitation, heme exposure, oxidative stress, desiccation, carbon fixation, anaerobic metabolism, or infection-relevant conditions. This score will allow the community to prioritize unstudied systems for future experimental work while remaining fully grounded in synthesis of public data.

The working group will create open tutorials and trainee-led analysis sprints focused on genome mining, public omics reanalysis, structural annotation, and reproducible workflow development. By unifying scattered datasets across organelle biology, metal homeostasis, redox metabolism, and microbial ecology, the project will reveal general principles by which molecular components self-organize into mesoscale cellular structures with new physiological capabilities.

abstract_original: Plant cytokinesis represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence. During this transient developmental window, molecular components—including cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, trans-Golgi network-derived vesicles, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a novel, higher-order structure: the cell plate. This highly dynamic process acts as a severe architectural bottleneck that is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly extreme temperature fluctuations and heat waves. While isolated studies have mapped individual components of the cytokinetic machinery or global plant stress responses, a massive knowledge gap remains: how do diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress? Addressing this complex phenomenon requires a scale of inquiry beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. We propose a community-scale data synthesis project, utilizing strictly publicly available data, to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience. Leveraging vast public repositories—such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), PRIDE, and various open-access bioimage databases—we will integrate spatiotemporal transcriptomes, vesicle proteomics, and cellular imaging across diverse plant systems ranging from key models like Arabidopsis to vital crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, to manage the immense scale and heterogeneity of these multi-omic data, we will deploy massively scalable, containerized computational workflows to process tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples uniformly. By applying advanced, noise-aware network construction toolkits, we will generate context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out confounding cross-dataset variables to isolate distinct regulatory modules that are activated exclusively at the intersection of specific times-of-day and high-temperature stress. We will bridge these transcriptomic network predictions to mesoscale cellular phenotypes by synthesizing public proteomic and image data, applying shape-based computational modeling to evaluate how environmental stress alters division-plane orientation, phragmoplast navigation, and unconventional protein secretion pathways. This transdisciplinary approach uniquely fuses chronobiology, endomembrane cell biology, and computational genomics. We aim to identify how the circadian clock temporally gates the trafficking of essential cell wall components during heat stress, and whether redundant genetic mechanisms reorganize the 4D temporal organellome to prevent catastrophic cell division failure. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative Working Group will not only answer fundamental questions about subcellular emergence but also serve as a premier training ground. Trainees will gain cutting-edge expertise at the intersection of biological synthesis, AI-driven network analysis, and scalable cloud computing. In strict adherence to open science principles, all resulting multi-omic matrices, context-specific networks, and reproducible computational pipelines will be made fully accessible to the global scientific community.

The three-dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome represents a profound emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale. Through the local coordination of epigenetic modifications, structural proteins, and transcription factors, linear DNA spontaneously folds into dynamic 3D architectures, such as loop domains and phase-separated hubs. These mesoscale structures ultimately dictate macroscopic cellular responses. Recent experimental advances have generated vast amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell chromatin conformation maps (e.g., Dip-C, Hi-C), single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). However, a critical synthesis gap remains: we lack a unified theoretical and computational framework that bridges the physical forces governing mesoscale chromatin architecture—specifically, the entropic and steric pressures exerted by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and pioneer factors—with systemic, genome-wide transcriptional outcomes. 

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the biophysical rules of emergent 3D genome architectures and their cascading effects on neuro-immune cellular plasticity. This working group will entirely leverage existing, publicly available data from the 4D Nucleome Project, the Human Cell Atlas, and GTEx. By integrating single-cell genomics, structural bioinformatics, and deep clinical transcriptomic profiling, our project aims to answer a longstanding mystery: how do local biophysical interactions, such as IDP-driven liquid-liquid phase separation and loop extrusion, generate the highly specific, emergent chromatin topologies required for coordinated cellular responses?

Our transdisciplinary approach is structured around three primary synthesis aims. First, we will utilize machine learning and AI-driven data science to fuse diverse multi-omic datasets (scRNA-seq, ATAC-seq, structural proteomics, and 3D genomics) across diverse human brain and immune cell types. This will create a unified, multi-layered atlas of cell-type-specific 3D genome configurations. Second, we will apply coarse-grained polymer physics modeling and biophysical simulations to these integrated datasets to infer the mechanical transmission and steric pressures exerted by IDPs and pioneer factors at domain boundaries. We hypothesize that biophysical parameters extracted from massive genomic datasets can reliably predict the physical thresholds required for chromatin opening and decompaction. Third, we will map these structural biophysical rules onto complex biological phenotypes, specifically analyzing how systemic perturbations—such as severe infection or neurological stress—remodel the genome's mesoscale architecture to drive maladaptive neuro-inflammatory and psychiatric phenotypes.

This synthesis project fundamentally demands the support of NCEMS, as it surpasses the capacity of any single laboratory by requiring the convergence of systems immunology, single-cell genomics, chromatin biophysics, and polymer physics. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, machine learning models, and polymer simulation pipelines will be made freely available as an open-source "Biophysical 3D-Omics" analytical suite. Furthermore, this working group will deeply integrate trainees, providing postdocs and graduate students with a unique, cross-disciplinary environment to master the synthesis of clinical multi-omics and theoretical biophysics, thereby training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore emergent biological complexity.

The unexpected appearance of new biological properties often occurs at the mesoscale, where distinct biomolecules assemble into complex functional modules. While mesoscale organization within individual cells is increasingly well-characterized, the emergence of cross-species mesoscale architectures—specifically, the structural and functional protein-protein interaction networks between human hosts and their resident microbiomes—remains a profound mystery. Understanding how these emergent host-microbiome interfaces assemble and evolve is critical to deciphering human systemic adaptations, yet it has been severely limited by computational bottlenecks, the prevalence of uncharacterized 'dark' microbial taxa, and the historic siloing of human proteomics and microbial metagenomics.

We propose a multidisciplinary Working Group to conduct a community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omic datasets, answering fundamental questions about the evolutionary emergence of mesoscale host-microbe protein networks. Our project integrates massive, disparate public databases: high-resolution human genomic and plasma proteomic cohorts (e.g., UK Biobank, providing data on thousands of circulating human proteins and their genetic regulators) alongside vast repositories of modern and ancient human metagenomic data (e.g., the Human Microbiome Project, ancient dental calculus, and paleofeces databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will deploy a novel, transdisciplinary analytical strategy using AI and data science to synthesize these existing resources.

To overcome the immense computational challenge of cross-kingdom alignment, we will leverage state-of-the-art, ultra-fast protein sequence alignment algorithms and advanced phylogenetic network modeling to process massive short-read datasets at a fraction of traditional computational costs. This infrastructure will map millions of microbial sequences—including those from understudied and ancestral microbial lineages—into a functionally annotated protein space. Crucially, by applying rigorous, gold-standard computational bio-filters derived from low-biomass microbiome research protocols, we will systematically exclude environmental contamination, ensuring that the inferred cross-species interactomes represent genuine biological interfaces.

We will then utilize AI-driven structural predictions and proteogenomic integration frameworks, such as cis-anchored protein mapping and Mendelian randomization, to model how these microbial proteins physically and functionally interact with the host systemic proteome. By comparing these proteogenomic networks across deep evolutionary time (ancient vs. modern humans) and diverse metabolic states (e.g., caloric restriction, multi-disease outcomes), we will uncover how emergent mesoscale properties—such as multi-protein metabolic sinks, host-mimicking immune complexes, and novel signaling hubs—have appeared and reorganized under evolutionary and environmental pressures.

This synthesis requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as it operates at a scale far beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. By bridging algorithmic phylogenetics, rigorous microbial ecology, and large-scale epidemiological proteomics, our Working Group will establish a new paradigm for studying biological emergence. The project strictly adheres to open science principles, committing to the FAIR release of all analytical pipelines, canonical network models, and integrated databases. Importantly, this initiative will cross-train a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists with the transdisciplinary expertise required to navigate complex multi-omic integration, algorithmic optimization, and rigorous contamination control.

The mesoscale organization of bacterial cells represents a critical frontier in molecular and cellular biosciences. While eukaryotic cells heavily rely on membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), the role of these emergent mesoscale structures in bacteria is only beginning to be recognized. Recent evidence suggests that bacteria utilize transient biomolecular condensates to coordinate stress responses, compartmentalize RNA-protein networks, and regulate host-microbe interactions. However, a major puzzle remains: how do dynamic fluctuations in gene expression and evolutionary mutations act as biophysical switches to trigger or dissolve these mesoscale assemblies? Addressing this requires integrating the principles of soft matter biophysics with systems-level bacterial genomics.

We propose to form an NCEMS Working Group that synthesizes massive, publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and structural datasets to construct the first comprehensive atlas of the "bacterial condensome." This project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating thousands of bacterial RNA-seq datasets (from GEO and SRA) covering diverse physiological states—including antibiotic exposure, host colonization, and quorum sensing—with genome-wide structural predictions from AlphaFold DB and intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) databases. 

By leveraging AI-driven biophysical models and associative polymer theory, our cross-disciplinary team will computationally map the sequence-encoded interaction potentials of bacterial proteomes. We will then overlay dynamic monomer concentrations derived from publicly available transcriptomic and proteomic data. A central challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences is bridging the gap between single-molecule biophysics and systems-level cellular behavior. While the thermodynamic constraints governing the biosynthesis, folding, and trafficking of individual proteins—such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ion channels—are increasingly well-characterized, we lack a predictive understanding of how these molecular-level energetic properties scale up to shape mesoscale protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, such as robust cellular homeostasis or the sudden collapse into pathological states like misfolding diseases and senescence, often originates at this poorly understood mesoscale level. 

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize three previously disconnected domains of publicly available data to uncover the thermodynamic rules governing mesoscale network emergence. Specifically, we will integrate (1) large-scale Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) and biophysical datasets capturing sequence-to-function thermodynamic landscapes; (2) structural interactome repositories including AlphaFold-predicted multimeric interfaces and public PPI databases; and (3) cell-type-specific transcriptomic atlases derived from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). By doing so, we aim to answer a fundamental question: How do localized energetic perturbations at protein interfaces propagate through complex cellular networks to drive emergent mesoscale phenotypes?

Our collaborative, transdisciplinary approach will proceed in three phases. First, we will aggregate and harmonize public DMS datasets with structural models to calculate how specific sequence variations alter the folding and binding free energies of membrane and intracellular proteins. Second, we will leverage advanced network science methodologies to map these energetic parameters onto mesoscale protein complexes. Rather than treating PPI networks as static binary connections, we will construct dynamically weighted, "energetic networks" that model the thermodynamic coupling between interacting proteins. Third, we will contextualize these biophysical networks using public scRNA-seq data. By applying gene regulatory network inference and cell-type-specific co-expression data, we will evaluate how the buffering capacity of different cellular environments modulates the penetrance of thermodynamic defects—explaining, for example, why identical mutations cause membrane supertrafficking in one cell type but induce targeted degradation or inflammatory stress responses in another.

This project requires the unique support of NCEMS, as it demands a synthesis of expertise in protein biophysics, structural biology, evolutionary dynamics, and computational systems biology that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory. The Working Group will adhere strictly to open science principles, releasing a novel, open-source analytical framework capable of predicting emergent cellular behaviors from primary sequence variation. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, providing postdocs and graduate students with cross-disciplinary expertise in synthesizing molecular thermodynamics, machine learning, and single-cell systems biology.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles formed by the liquid liquid phase separation of RNAs and proteins represent an important mesoscale biological organization with well documented compositional components. A unified framework connecting atomic level RNA protein interactions and sequence features to the emergent mesoscale physical properties, dynamic trafficking, and physical functions of these condensates is currently lacking. This project will synthesize multimodal datasets to build a predictive computational framework linking atomic scale interactions to mesoscale properties through a three phase approach involving Rosetta modeling, graph theoretic networks, and DAPTEV deep learning. Extracted structural features from PDB and EMDB repositories will form a matrix overlaid onto multilayered proteome trafficking networks built from PRIDE and proximity labeling datasets for correlation with CondenSeq imaging data. This predictive framework will connect atomistic models to soft matter physics, enabling phase transition predictions from sequence variants to inform studies on cellular stress and age related protein aggregation diseases.
full_text: This research investigates mesoscale biological organization of biomolecular condensates to address missing links between atomic interactions and physical properties. The components of biomolecular condensates are documented but the impact of atomic alterations on dynamic trafficking remains poorly understood. The proposed study builds a predictive computational framework connecting atomic interactions to material properties to study age related diseases. The study design integrates structural features from public datasets into proteomic networks and uses machine learning to predict material properties. The project applies specific tools for macromolecular modeling (Rosetta) alongside algorithms of graph theory and models of deep learning. Biomolecular condensates represent a canonical example of mesoscale emergence in biology, where non-stoichiometric assemblies of RNAs and proteins phase separate to form dynamically regulated, membraneless organelles. While the compositional landscape of condensates—such as stress granules and nuclear speckles—is increasingly well-documented, a fundamental mechanistic gap remains: we lack a predictive understanding of how atomic-scale RNA-protein interactions and protein sequence determinants scale up to dictate emergent, mesoscale material properties like viscoelasticity, interfacial tension, and dynamic subcellular trafficking. Currently, a massive amount of disconnected, publicly available data exists across diverse domains. These include high-resolution structural repositories (PDB, EMDB) capturing RNA-protein complexes, high-throughput pooled imaging datasets linking protein sequences to condensate phenotypes, and extensive dynamic spatial proteomics (e.g., BioID, APEX, and proximity-labeling networks) tracking proteome trafficking. 

We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize these disparate, multi-modal datasets into a unified, predictive computational framework of mesoscale condensate emergence. Relying entirely on existing publicly available data, our transdisciplinary team will bridge computational structural biology, RNA modeling, soft matter physics, and cellular proteomics. First, we will leverage advanced macromolecular modeling (e.g., Rosetta-based frameworks) and deep learning algorithms to extract high-confidence structural signatures—such as RNA-protein interaction interfaces, multivalent valency maps, and RNA folding architectures—from existing cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps and structural databases. Second, we will map these structural metrics onto dynamic, spatial interactomes derived from public proximity-labeling proteomics datasets. This synthesis will allow us to reconstruct the precise spatiotemporal trafficking networks of phase-separating proteins and their RNA scaffolds across varying cellular conditions, such as oxidative stress and environmental fluctuations.

Finally, we will integrate soft matter physics principles to correlate these derived structural networks with the tunable, emergent material properties documented in public high-throughput imaging screens. By identifying the underlying "grammar" of multi-component condensate networks, we aim to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how specific sequence properties and chaperone interactions dictate the assembly, maintenance, and dissolution of these mesoscale compartments. 

This synthesis project requires the unique collaborative environment of NCEMS, as it extends beyond the computational or biological capacity of a single lab. It will yield an open-access, integrated database and predictive analytical pipeline linking atomic structures to emergent cellular phenotypes. Furthermore, it will directly address the NCEMS mission by developing a new analytical strategy for understanding mesoscale biological systems, while providing a rich, collaborative training ground for postdocs and graduate students in the integration of structural bioinformatics, AI-driven macromolecular modeling, and spatial omics data.

Biomolecular condensates represent a primary mode of mesoscale spatial organization across all domains of life, governing processes ranging from eukaryotic stress adaptation to bacterial subcellular compartmentalization. While recent years have seen an explosion of data cataloging phase-separating proteins, predicting the emergent physical properties of these assemblies—such as ultrastructural organization, emulsion stability, and tunable viscoelasticity—from primary sequence remains a critical frontier. Current efforts largely focus on binary predictions of liquid-liquid phase separation, failing to capture the intricate biophysical rules that dictate how condensates dynamically respond to environmental fluctuations, resist coalescence, and maintain complex multiphase architectures within the crowded cellular milieu.

This working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the pan-domain molecular grammar underlying condensate ultrastructure and mesoscale emergence. By aggregating and synthesizing disparate, publicly available datasets—including curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence repositories (DisProt), structural data (AlphaFold DB, EMDB for cryo-ET maps), and thousands of published in vitro biophysical measurements (phase diagrams, zeta potentials, and rheological parameters)—we will construct a unified, predictive framework of condensate physics. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, our approach relies entirely on the integration of existing multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, requiring no new experimental generation.

To achieve this, we will combine artificial intelligence with physics-driven multiscale computational modeling. First, we will develop a machine-learning pipeline to mine sequence features, specifically mapping the 'stickers-and-spacers' valency and electrostatic charge patterning of IDPs across diverse biological kingdoms. We will correlate these specific sequence grammars with documented emergent behaviors, such as RNA-induced conformational switching, multiphase coexistence, and hydration-dependent structural transitions. Second, we will leverage these synthesized datasets to parameterize high-throughput, sequence-dependent coarse-grained molecular models. This will allow us to simulate mesoscale phenomena—such as long-ranged electrostatic repulsion, surface charge-driven size control, and fusion propensity—at an unprecedented scale. By triangulating these physical simulations with published ultrastructural readouts, we will determine how localized structural transitions and net charge within dense phases dictate higher-order cellular functions.

This transdisciplinary effort uniquely bridges structural biology, computational biophysics, and soft matter physics. The project requires the NCEMS infrastructure to facilitate the large-scale integration of highly heterogeneous data types (from atomic coordinates to rheological values) and to support the collaborative computational demands of parameterizing pan-domain physical models. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how intrinsically disordered sequences encode mesoscale architecture, generating predictive tools that map the physical rules of cellular adaptation. Furthermore, the project will train a diverse new generation of data-savvy biophysicists equipped to navigate the intersection of machine learning, polymer physics, and structural biology, fully embracing open science principles by releasing all analytical workflows, trained AI models, and coarse-grained parameters to the global community.

Rather than arising from isolated molecular events, these adaptive traits emerge from the dynamic reorganization of 3D chromatin architectures (e.g., enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA assemblies) and the subsequent rewiring of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks. Despite the sheer volume of public multi-omics data, understanding how distributed genetic variations and secondary genetic modifiers synergistically perturb these mesoscale assemblies to drive variable disease expressivity remains a long-standing mystery. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the multiscale mechanisms underlying cancer plasticity and immune-checkpoint efficacy. By synthesizing vast, publicly available datasets—including ENCODE, TCGA, CCLE/DepMap, DICE, and large-scale CRISPR/Cas9 cellular screens—we will build an AI-driven computational framework that connects 1D sequence variation to emergent cellular outcomes. Our synthesis approach is structured across three integrated aims. First, we will map how primary driver mutations and secondary genetic modifiers dictate lineage-specific 3D genome organization. By leveraging single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell eQTL data, and 3D chromatin conformation maps, we will employ advanced sequence-to-function statistical learning to model the assembly of mesoscale regulatory hubs. We will specifically focus on how extrachromosomal DNA and structural variants override traditional topological boundaries to drive oncogenic and immunosuppressive transcriptional programs. Second, we will bridge the gap between 3D chromatin dysregulation and mesoscale protein complex dynamics. Using positive-unlabeled (PU) machine learning and ensemble-based scoring functions for protein-protein docking, we will predict how altered gene expression profiles and variant-driven misfolding events reshape protein interaction networks. This will allow us to map the hierarchy of protein complex stability and identify interaction nodes that act as functional hubs during cellular adaptation. Finally, we will link these mesoscale reconfigurations to emergent cellular outcomes, specifically the variable expressivity of immune escape in T cell subsets and breast cancer models. By analyzing transcriptomic and structural tumor-immune interaction networks, we will pinpoint the epigenetic and structural determinants that curtail targeted therapy and immunotherapy efficacy. The emergence of mesoscale cellular architecture—such as the dynamic assembly, architectural scaling, and targeted shedding of organelles—relies on the continuous reorganization of underlying cytoskeletal networks. While the molecular constituents, such as actin, microtubules, and motor proteins, are heavily studied, the biophysical rules dictating how these stochastic microscale interactions scale up to control whole-organelle structural decisions (e.g., centriole symmetry breaking, rapid ciliary deciliation, and cytokinetic ring compaction) remain deeply elusive. The recent explosion of publicly available volumetric imaging atlases and multidimensional live-cell time-series datasets presents an unprecedented opportunity to solve this long-standing puzzle. However, these repositories are highly heterogeneous in spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and imaging modality, preventing traditional analytical approaches from extracting unifying biophysical principles. 

This Working Group proposes to uncover the emergent properties of cytoskeleton-driven organelle remodeling through the community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available whole-cell imaging and time-series datasets (such as those from EMPIAR, the Allen Cell Observatory, and systematically curated cell anatomy literature databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will bridge the gap between static, high-resolution structural snapshots and complex, dynamic live-cell trajectories. 

To achieve this synthesis, our transdisciplinary team will integrate AI-driven image analysis with advanced mathematical modeling. First, we will deploy deep learning auto-segmentation pipelines to extract quantitative 3D morphometrics—such as surface curvature, volume, and cytoskeletal network connectivity—from vast datasets of whole-cell soft X-ray and electron tomograms. Second, to synthesize dynamic temporal data across varying experimental platforms, we will implement scalable Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport metrics. This innovative mathematical framework allows us to align unequally spaced, multidimensional biological time series into a unified state space, calculating barycenters that represent consensus trajectories of mesoscale organelle remodeling.

These generalized structural trajectories will subsequently serve as rigorous empirical constraints for stochastic, agent-based biophysical models. By simulating the intricate interactions between cytoskeletal filaments and diverse motor protein populations, we will computationally test competing hypotheses regarding organelle biogenesis and disassembly. To efficiently explore the vast parameter space of these constrained models, we will utilize Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation, directly linking computational outputs to the synthetic optimal transport trajectories derived from public data. This closed-loop analytical strategy will reveal how specific microscale parameter shifts (e.g., altered motor binding kinetics or localized substrate depletion) spontaneously trigger macroscopic morphological changes like whole-cilium shedding or single-site centriole biogenesis.

Addressing these fundamental questions of mesoscale emergence requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as this synthesis spans computer vision, optimal transport mathematics, agent-based biophysics, and organelle cell biology—a scope far beyond the capabilities of any individual laboratory. Adhering strictly to open science principles, all integrated datasets, optimal transport algorithms, and parameterized biophysical models will be published openly. Finally, this project will provide immersive cross-disciplinary training for graduate students and postdocs, preparing a new workforce of data-savvy scientists capable of interrogating biological emergence through the integration of AI and complex systems mathematics.

Emergence in biological systems frequently stems from the spatial and functional organization of individual molecular interactions into higher-order mesoscale architectures. In molecular biology, the clustering of transcription factor (TF) binding events within dynamic chromatin landscapes forms robust regulatory domains that control cell-type identity. A long-standing mystery in cellular sciences is how these complex mesoscale regulatory networks emerge evolutionarily to drive genomic innovation. Transposable elements (TEs)—highly repetitive DNA sequences that mobilize throughout genomes—are increasingly hypothesized to be primary engines of this emergence, functioning as distributed, ready-to-use TF binding modules that nucleate new regulatory hubs. However, the collective mechanism by which species-specific TEs collaboratively rewire chromatin at the mesoscale remains critically under-explored.

A major barrier to understanding TE-driven emergence is methodological: sequence divergence and the repetitive nature of TEs severely confound cross-species alignment and predictive modeling. Individual research groups lack the diverse expertise and computational infrastructure required to synthesize the vast arrays of fragmented, publicly available epigenomic data necessary to resolve this puzzle. To address this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of ultra-high-resolution, publicly available epigenomic datasets—spanning ChIP-seq, ChIP-exo, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq—across multiple mammalian lineages. 

By uniting experts in computational epigenomics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning, this NCEMS-supported collaboration will deploy advanced domain-adaptive neural networks to synthesize these diverse datasets. These sophisticated AI architectures are specifically designed to correct for evolutionary domain shifts caused by species-specific repeats, enabling accurate, cross-species prediction and imputation of TF binding and chromatin states. Applying integrative state annotation algorithms across these standardized datasets, we aim to answer three fundamental questions: (1) How do coordinated arrays of TEs collectively nucleate emergent mesoscale chromatin structures, such as robust enhancer clusters? (2) What are the specific sequence and chromatin determinants that allow a newly transposed element to transition along a continuum—from an isolated molecular binding event to an integrated, cooperative node within a cell-type-specific regulatory network? (3) How do these mesoscale structural innovations dictate higher-order cellular outcomes, using well-profiled systems like multi-lineage hematopoiesis as our model framework?

This project fully embraces the NCEMS mandate for open science and reproducible synthesis. Our pipelines will be embedded within flexible, web-based bioinformatics management platforms (e.g., Galaxy-integrated environments) to ensure rigorous quality control and full reproducibility across thousands of public datasets. Furthermore, the Working Group will serve as an essential training incubator. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, transdisciplinary ecosystem, we will train a diverse, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain unparalleled hands-on experience at the intersection of artificial intelligence, high-throughput epigenomics, and evolutionary theory, ultimately equipping the next generation of scientists to decode the emergent properties of the cell.

abstract_text: Mesoscale biology investigates the structural architecture and dynamic interactions of multi protein assemblies, rendering abundant physical distance constraints from crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets essential for advancing structural systems biology. Current systems biology models lack spatial constraints and structural techniques lack cellular context, while existing mass spectrometry datasets remain highly fragmented and rely on inconsistent error estimation models. The primary objective is to synthesize crosslinking mass spectrometry data into a three dimensional tissue specific interactome; computationally, this project will extract constraints using sequence search engines, integrate AlphaFold2 Multimer predictions, and apply network propagation algorithms. Standardized crosslinking measurements from ProteomeXchange and PRIDE will be merged with tissue specific abundance atlases and Reactome databases, paired with structural predictions, and overlaid with UK Biobank genome wide association data. This research will output standardized methodologies for structural multi omics integration, providing a mechanistic explanation for how pleiotropic genetic variants disrupt physical architecture and cause cellular dysfunction.

The transition from individual biomolecules to functional organelles is governed by emergent mesoscale properties, which are largely driven by dynamic protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and multi-protein assemblies. While traditional systems biology has mapped cellular networks, these models often lack the spatial resolution required to understand the physical constraints and architectural emergence of mesoscale complexes. Over the past decade, Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) has emerged as a powerful technique to capture direct physical distance constraints within and between proteins in their native cellular environments. Thousands of such datasets currently reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain severely fragmented, lacking harmonized error estimation, standardized metadata, and integration with broader cellular networks, thereby obscuring our view of mesoscale biology.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to systematically re-process, harmonize, and integrate the global public archive of XL-MS data to uncover the structural architecture of emergent mesoscale assemblies. By leveraging standardized frameworks such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF), our transdisciplinary working group will extract and validate high-confidence, spatially resolved PPIs from billions of mass spectra deposited across global repositories like ProteomeXchange. We will synthesize these structural distance constraints with existing tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases to build a comprehensive, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell.

This synthesized structural interactome will allow us to address long-standing questions regarding mesoscale emergence: How do localized protein interactions dynamically scale to form stable multimeric complexes and organelle contact sites across different human tissues? To connect these biophysical properties to human health, we will integrate our structural networks with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Using network-propagation analysis, we will map how disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants specifically perturb the physical architecture of these mesoscale assemblies, altering their emergent properties and downstream cellular outcomes.

This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. It relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental data generation. The massive computational scale of re-analyzing disparate XL-MS archives, combined with the required cross-disciplinary fusion of biophysics, bioinformatics standardization, and network genetics, makes this endeavor impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, data scientists, and systems biologists. In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized datasets, spatial networks, and programmatic pipelines will be disseminated via public REST APIs and integrated into community resources. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground, equipping early-career researchers with advanced skills in multi-omics integration, structural modeling, and big data harmonization, ultimately training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore the frontiers of mesoscale biology.

abstract_text: In microbial ecosystems, operons encode mesoscale multi enzyme protein complexes that generate specialized metabolites, representing an important biological phenomenon that yields extensive public omics data from uncultured organisms. The current scientific gap is the inability to connect novel microbial protein structures to their chemical products because of isolated datasets and restricted culture biased reference databases. This project will build a reference free computational network connecting uncultured microbiome genetic sequences to biochemical outputs by synthesizing datasets using alignment free neural networks, evolutionary reconstruction models, and machine learning association models. The research will integrate Sequence Read Archive metagenomes with PRIDE spectra by applying machine learning and large scale co occurrence analyses to paired multi omic metadata. This project will produce a reference free computational network that maps unannotated genetic information directly to chemical phenotypes, enabling the identification of previously unrecognized biological and chemical data.
